  • Deut. 14:1. "Ye are the children of the LORD your God" — the idiom confirmed by usage: God's covenant people are His sons; "sons of God" names the faithful line, sealing the Sethite reading of Gen. 6:2.
  • PP 81.2. White: "For some time the two classes remained separate... So long as this separation continued, they maintained the worship of God in its purity. But in the lapse of time they ventured, little by little, to mingle... Mingling with the depraved, they became like them in spirit and in deeds; the restrictions of the seventh commandment were disregarded, 'and they took them wives of all which they chose'" — the confirming witness names "the two classes," quotes Gen. 6:2 as the covenant line's fall through intermarriage, and states outright that the seventh commandment was disregarded: Lamech's plurality now the practice of the professed people of God, the first institution debased and the distinction dissolved with it.

The second blow — appetite made the horizon of life — Matt. 24:38-39; Luke 17:27; Gen. 9:3:

  • Matt. 24:38. "For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark" — Christ names the mark of the heedless class: not scandalous crime but lawful things — eating, drinking, marrying — made the whole of life; appetite made the horizon.
    • eating and drinking = Christ's mark of the heedless class before the flood: lawful appetite made the whole of life, so that the ordinary swallowed the eternal and men "knew not" until judgment fell (Matt. 24:38-39; Luke 17:27) — the sign of a world that has erased the distinction between the holy and the common. Defined in full at the close.
  • Luke 17:27. "They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all" — Luke piles the verbs: eat, drank, married — the tempo of a life wholly given to the permitted, right up to the shut door. The same class Christ warns will be present at His coming (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling").
  • Gen. 9:3. "Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things" — the proof-text of the whole appetite argument: only AFTER the flood is flesh granted. Through the entire antediluvian age the Gen. 1:29 grant still stood; the world "did eat, they drank" in violation of, not permission for, the original diet.
  • 3SM 289.1. White: "The flesh of dead animals was not the original food for man. Man was permitted to eat it after the Flood because all vegetation had been destroyed" — confirms the grant-boundary exactly as Gen. 1:29 against Gen. 9:3: flesh was no part of the Eden table, and the permission is post-flood.
  • DA 636.2. White: "The crisis is stealing gradually upon us... Men are still eating and drinking, planting and building, marrying, and giving in marriage... yet probation's hour is fast closing" — the heedless-class pattern of Matt. 24:38 carried to the end: the same absorption in the lawful while the door swings shut.

The third blow — appointed worship: the way of Cain runs to the end:

  • The war on the third institution was already open when Cain brought his self-appointed offering and God refused it (Gen. 4:3-5 — the ground walked in "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"). Scripture records no antediluvian Sabbath-breaking, and none is claimed here; what it records is the principle — worship on man's terms against worship on God's terms — and that war does not close with the flood. It runs down the whole controversy and meets the Sabbath of Gen. 2:1-3 at the end, where the appointed rest becomes the visible line between the two classes (Rev. 13-14; see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible").

The fruit of the threefold assault — one apostate mass — Gen. 6:5:

  • Gen. 6:5. "And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" — the fruit of the threefold assault: with marriage debased, appetite enthroned, and worship self-appointed, the whole earth becomes one apostate mass — save one household.

Noah — the distinction kept, and remade by God's own hand — 2 Pet. 2:5; Gen. 6:3; Heb. 11:7; Gen. 6:22; Matt. 24:39; Gen. 7:16:

  • 2 Pet. 2:5. "And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly" — the one preserved witness: "a preacher of righteousness," the peculiar line that would not be absorbed. Eighth person: the remnant few against "the world of the ungodly."
  • Gen. 6:3. "My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years" — Scripture dates the window itself: 120 years of striving Spirit before the judgment, the measured probation of the mingled world.
  • 4T 308.3. White: "Noah preached to the people of his time that God would give them one hundred and twenty years in which to repent of their sins and find refuge in the ark, but they refused the gracious invitation" — the Gen. 6:3 window preached: 120 years of warning refused, so the world's "knew not" (Matt. 24:39) was willful; they had Noah's preaching and rejected it.
  • Heb. 11:7. "By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith" — the ark itself, built by faith, "condemned the world": Noah's obedience redrew the line the world had blurred, and his righteousness is the righteousness of faith.
  • Gen. 6:22. "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he" — the obedience that condemned the world stated plainly: ALL that God commanded. The peculiar people are marked by keeping the commandments the mingled world neglected.
  • Matt. 24:39. "And knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" — the mingled world's ignorance is willful ignorance; the judgment remakes the distinction they had erased. Christ fixes the pattern on the last day.
  • Gen. 7:16. "And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in" — "the LORD shut him in": the distinction the mingling dissolved is remade by God's own hand at the judgment. Probation closes by divine act, not human choice — the shut-in faithful, the shut-out world.
  • EP 55.4. White: "Noah and his household were within the ark, 'and the Lord shut him in.' The massive door, impossible for those within to close, was slowly swung to its place by unseen hands. Noah was shut in and the rejecters of God's mercy were shut out" — confirms Gen. 7:16 as the close of probation dividing the two classes: one door, two sides, God's hand on it.
  • EW 284.1. White: "When the rain descended and the flood came, Noah and his family had entered the ark, and God had shut them in... God would not suffer the wicked to destroy those who... would not bow to the decree of the beast or receive his mark" — the inspired bridge to the end: the shut-in distinction of Noah's day is the very deliverance of those who refuse the beast's decree — the last mingling and the last separation (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling"; "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible").

DEFINITION — THE DAYS OF NOAH — THE INSTITUTIONS OF EDEN UNDER ATTACK = before sin God gave three gifts, the institutions of Eden: marriage — one man, one woman, one flesh (Gen. 2:24); the appointed diet — the seed-bearing herbs, fruits, and grains, flesh absent (Gen. 1:29; enlarged to the herb of the field after the fall, Gen. 3:18); and the Sabbath — the seventh day blessed and sanctified (Gen. 2:1-3) — marriage and the Sabbath "twin institutions" born in Eden (AH 340.4), Sabbath and family "indissolubly linked" (Ed 250.2), the Creator's chosen diet confirmed (CD 81.2). By Noah's day the serpent's seed had struck them in order: marriage by Lamech's polygamy in Cain's line (Gen. 4:19) and then by the covenant line itself — the sons of God, the line of Seth (Luke 3:38; Deut. 14:1), taking "wives of all which they chose" while "the restrictions of the seventh commandment were disregarded" (Gen. 6:2; PP 81.2); appetite by eating and drinking made the whole of life (Matt. 24:38; Luke 17:27) — and since flesh was not granted until after the flood (Gen. 9:3; 3SM 289.1), the antediluvian table itself ran against the still-standing grant of Eden; and appointed worship by the way of Cain's self-chosen offering (Gen. 4:3-5) — worship on man's terms against worship on God's terms — a war that meets the Sabbath only at the end (Rev. 13-14). The fruit was total: "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen. 6:5) — save Noah, "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Pet. 2:5) through the 120-year window God Himself had set (Gen. 6:3; 4T 308.3), whose ark-building faith "condemned the world" (Heb. 11:7) because he did "according to all that God commanded him" (Gen. 6:22). Then the distinction the mingling had erased was remade by God's own hand: "the LORD shut him in" (Gen. 7:16; EP 55.4) while the world that "knew not" was taken away (Matt. 24:39) — and Christ stakes the last age on the same pattern, when those who will not bow to the beast's decree are shut in as Noah was (EW 284.1): "so shall also the coming of the Son of man be."

Symbols defined here:

  • the institutions of Eden = the three gifts God established before sin: MARRIAGE (one man and one woman made one flesh), the APPOINTED DIET (the seed-bearing bounty given for meat), and the SABBATH (the seventh day blessed and sanctified) — all three predating the fall, all three assaulted by the serpent's seed: polygamy against marriage, indulgence against the diet, self-appointed worship against the appointed, the last war ending at the Sabbath (Gen. 2:24; Gen. 1:29; Gen. 2:1-3; Gen. 4:19; Gen. 6:2).
  • the original diet = the Gen. 1:29 grant — fruits, grains, herbs, and after the fall the herb of the field — with flesh not granted until after the flood, so that the vegetable grant stood through the whole antediluvian age and the days-of-Noah appetite ran against, not within, God's appointment (Gen. 1:29; Gen. 3:18; Gen. 9:3).
  • eating and drinking = Christ's mark of the heedless class before the flood: lawful appetite — eating, drinking, marrying — made the whole of life, so that the ordinary swallowed the eternal and men "knew not" until judgment fell; not gross crime but total absorption in the permitted, the sign of a world that has erased the distinction between the holy and the common (Matt. 24:38-39; Luke 17:27).

Symbols carried: the sons of God, the daughters of men, and the mingling — the alliance by which the peculiar people lost their peculiarity (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); Cain's offering and the way of Cain — the first war on appointed worship, whose antediluvian record is the altar, not the Sabbath (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"); the city of Cain and Lamech's polygamy — the civilization that carried the attack (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); the two seeds and the God-put enmity the mingling dissolved (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"). Forward: Christ's days-of-Noah pattern for the last generation (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling") and the worship war's terminus at seal versus mark (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible").

For discussion:

  1. Every count against the antediluvian world in Matt. 24:38 is a LAWFUL thing — "eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage" — yet "the flood came, and took them all away." How does the permitted become the destroyer, and where in your own week has a lawful thing quietly become the whole of life?
  2. Flesh was not granted until after the flood (Gen. 9:3), so the antediluvians' indulgence ran against a standing grant of God (Gen. 1:29). Where do we treat God's later concessions as if they erased His original appointments — in appetite, in marriage, in rest — and what would returning toward "the life of Eden" (Ed 250.2) cost this week?
  3. Noah "condemned the world" not by argument but by obedience — an ark built to "all that God commanded him" (Heb. 11:7; Gen. 6:22) — and then "the LORD shut him in" (Gen. 7:16). If the distinction between the two classes is finally remade by God's hand and not ours, what is our part now, before the door — and what was the world's part during Noah's 120 years of warning?

Part III — The Witnesses Repeat

¶6. Babel — Congregating for Convenience

The first post-flood act of the serpent's seed is to rebuild the city: "let us build us a city... lest we be scattered" is open defiance of "replenish the earth," and God answers the congregation with the very scattering it was built to prevent — naming the whole system Babel, CONFUSION, the name it carries all the way to Revelation.

The command Babel defies — "replenish the earth" — Gen. 9:1, 19:

  • Gen. 9:1. "And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth" — God's post-flood word is centrifugal: fill the earth, spread out. Every clause of Babel's manifesto is written against this one command; the whole plot is congregation against dispersal.
  • Gen. 9:19. "These are the three sons of Noah: and of them was the whole earth overspread" — God's design is that the whole earth be OVERSPREAD from Noah's sons. Scattering is the blessing, not the curse; the Babel-builders want the exact opposite.

The city is Cain's signature — and the Name is Seth's — Gen. 4:16-17, 26:

  • Gen. 4:16-17. "And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD... and he builded a city" — the first city-builder in Scripture is the first man who went out from the presence of the LORD. City-founding is the serpent-seed's signature act — safety and a name apart from God (the city of Cain is defined in "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); Babel is the same impulse resurrected after the flood.
  • Gen. 4:26. "then began men to call upon the name of the LORD" — Seth's line calls upon the NAME OF THE LORD. Set this exactly against Babel's "let us make us a name" (Gen. 11:4): the two seeds are divided by whose name is invoked — the Name called upon, or the name made.

Nimrod — the founder named — Gen. 10:8-12; Mic. 5:6:

  • Gen. 10:8-9. "And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD" — the founder named: a mighty hunter before — in the face of — the LORD; might in defiance, not in worship.
  • Gen. 10:10. "And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar" — Babel is the HEADWATER: the first post-flood kingdom, founded by Nimrod son of Cush on the plain of Shinar in the first generations after the ark.
  • Gen. 10:11-12. "Out of that land went forth Asshur, and builded Nineveh" — from Shinar the city-system multiplies outward, city upon city compounding into "a great city" (Gen. 10:12). The confederacy of great cities is the fruit of Nimrod's Babel, and the pattern runs straight to "Babylon the great, that great city" of Revelation.
  • Mic. 5:6. "And they shall waste the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in the entrances thereof" — Scripture itself calls the enemy-land "the land of Nimrod": the Bible's own witness that Nimrod's Babel names the archetypal oppressor-kingdom, the confederated power against God's people.

Down from the mountains to the plain of Shinar — Gen. 11:1-2:

  • Gen. 11:1. "And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech" — the pre-Babel condition: total unity of speech. Unity is not itself the sin; the sin is unity harnessed against the command of God.
  • Gen. 11:2. "as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there" — they stop journeying and settle on the plain: the geography of Cain's line, the lowland against the mountains of the faithful (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"). To "dwell there" is to refuse to be scattered.
  • EP 70.3. White: "For a time, the descendants of Noah continued to dwell among the mountains where the ark had rested. As their numbers increased, apostasy led to division... After a time they decided to separate. Accordingly they journeyed to Shinar" — the mountain/plain division of the two classes re-enacted after the flood: the apostate line separates from the worshipers of God and descends to the plain.
  • 8MR 42.1. White: "Those who desired to forget their Creator, and to cast off the restraint of His law, decided to separate from the worshipers of God... Thus they hoped to make themselves independent of God" — the split named at its headwater: apostasy led to division, and Babel is the serpent-seed's congregation, built to be "independent of God."

Brick for stone, a tower for safety, a name for themselves — Gen. 11:3-4:

  • Gen. 11:3. "Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter" — man-made brick for God-made stone, slime for mortar: the whole enterprise is substitution, human manufacture standing in for what God provides — a self-made security.
  • Gen. 11:4. "Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth" — the manifesto in one verse: (1) "a city and a tower" — congregation for convenience and safety in numbers; (2) "make us a name" — self-exaltation against calling on the LORD's name (Gen. 4:26); (3) "lest we be scattered" — explicit defiance of Gen. 9:1. Every clause is against a word of God.
    • Babel / Babylon = the serpent-seed's confederated city-system: congregation for convenience and self-security in defiance of God's command to fill the earth, and self-naming in defiance of calling on the Name of the LORD (Gen. 11:4 against Gen. 9:1 and Gen. 4:26); founded by Nimrod on the plain of Shinar — "the beginning of his kingdom was Babel" (Gen. 10:10) — named CONFUSION by God's own judgment (Gen. 11:9), and carried by the Spirit to its end-time head as "BABYLON THE GREAT" (Rev. 17:5). Defined in full at the close.
    • the tower = man-made security against God's judgment and against God's command to scatter and fill the earth — brick-and-slime presumption trusted for the safety and the name that belong to the LORD alone, so small the LORD must "come down" to see it, answered by the very scattering it was built to prevent (Gen. 11:3-5; Gen. 11:8). Defined in full at the close.
  • PP 119.1. White: "One object before them in the erection of the tower was to secure their own safety in case of another deluge... The whole undertaking was designed to exalt still further the pride of its projectors and to turn the minds of future generations away from God and lead them into idolatry" — the tower-symbol confirmed exactly: man-made security against God's judgment, born of pride and unbelief in God's covenant word. The same paragraph supplies the seed-continuity: "their hearts, like that of Cain, rose up in rebellion against Him" (PP 119.1) — the Babel-builders' hearts are Cain's heart, one line from Cain's city (Gen. 4:17) to Nimrod's plain (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall").
  • EP 70.4. White: "God had directed men to disperse throughout the earth, but these Babel builders determined to keep their community united and to found a monarchy that should embrace the whole earth" — the defiance of Gen. 9:1 named: God said disperse; Babel said stay united and build a universal empire — the metropolis and the monument of its builders' power.

"Go to, let us go down" — the confederacy broken — Gen. 11:5-9:

  • Gen. 11:5. "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded" — the tower that was to "reach unto heaven" is so small the LORD must "come down" to see it. The irony judges the pride: man cannot climb to God by masonry.
  • Gen. 11:6. "Behold, the people is one... and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do" — unbroken confederacy makes evil limitless. God scatters not from spite but to restrain corporate rebellion, as He divided the seeds at the first (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall").
  • Gen. 11:7. "Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language" — God answers "Go to, let us build" with His own "Go to, let us go down." The confounding of speech is the instrument of the scattering the builders feared.
  • Gen. 11:8. "So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city" — the exact thing they built to prevent, God accomplishes. The distinction between the two classes is remade by judgment, as at Eden's gate and at the flood.
  • Gen. 11:9. "Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth" — they sought a name; God gave them one — Babel, CONFUSION. The self-made name becomes the byword of judgment, and this naming is inherited by the whole city-system of Revelation.
  • EP 71.1. White: "Angels were sent to bring to naught the purpose of the builders... the language was confounded so that the directions delivered were often the reverse of those that had been given... Lightnings from heaven as an evidence of God's displeasure broke off the upper portion of the tower" — corroborates Gen. 11:7-8: God's direct judgment confounds the speech and breaks the tower, accomplishing the scattering the builders built against.

From Babel to Babylon the great — the city-system at full stature — Rev. 17:5; 18:4:

  • Rev. 17:5. "And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH" — the headwater of Shinar grown to the end-time confederacy of the serpent's seed: still self-named, still congregated against God, and Scripture names her by Babel's name — "the mother" of the whole system.
  • TMR 37.2. Andrews: "The word Babylon signifies confusion, and is derived from Babel... being the chosen term of the Holy Spirit to designate 'that mighty city'... was doubtless selected with especial reference to its signification" — the pioneer definition sealing the Babel-to-Babylon line: Babylon = confusion = Babel, the Spirit's own chosen name for the Revelation city, "composed of professed worshipers of God."
  • TMR 47.2. Andrews: "Since the great apostasy, the majority of the professed followers have busied themselves in attempting to climb up to heaven some other way. They have been confounded in the attempt, and scattered abroad... with creeds as discordant as the languages of those who were dispersed at the ancient tower" — the antitype drawn: the great apostasy repeats Babel's tower, climbing to heaven another way, and ends in the same confusion.
  • Rev. 18:4. "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues" — the final answer to Babel's "lest we be scattered": God still scatters His people OUT of the city of confusion before He judges it — the everlasting separation of the two seeds (see "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

DEFINITION — BABEL — CONGREGATING FOR CONVENIENCE = the first post-flood act of the serpent's seed is to rebuild the city, and every clause of the rebuilding is written against a word of God. God's blessing was centrifugal — "replenish the earth" (Gen. 9:1), the whole earth "overspread" from Noah's sons (Gen. 9:19) — but the apostate line, hearts "like that of Cain" (PP 119.1; Gen. 4:16-17), separated from the worshipers of God, descended from the mountains to the plain of Shinar (Gen. 11:2; EP 70.3; 8MR 42.1), and under Nimrod, the mighty hunter before the LORD whose kingdom began at Babel (Gen. 10:8-10; Mic. 5:6), raised a city and a tower of brick and slime (Gen. 11:3): congregation for convenience ("let us build us a city"), self-exaltation against the Name called upon by Seth's line ("let us make us a name," Gen. 11:4 against Gen. 4:26), and open defiance of the scattering ("lest we be scattered abroad"). The tower was man-made security against God's judgment and monument to its builders' pride (PP 119.1; EP 70.4) — yet so small the LORD must "come down" to see it (Gen. 11:5). Because unbroken confederacy makes evil limitless (Gen. 11:6), God answered "let us build" with "let us go down" (Gen. 11:7), confounded the speech, broke the tower (EP 71.1), and accomplished by judgment the very scattering the congregation was built to prevent — the distinction between the two classes remade, as at Eden's gate and at the flood, and the self-made name turned to CONFUSION: Babel (Gen. 11:8-9). That name the Spirit carries to the end: the city-system of Shinar reaches full stature as "BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS" (Rev. 17:5; TMR 37.2), the great apostasy repeating the tower — climbing to heaven another way, confounded into discordant creeds (TMR 47.2) — until God's final answer to "lest we be scattered" falls: "Come out of her, my people" (Rev. 18:4). The witnesses repeat: the serpent's seed congregates for convenience; God's people are content to be scattered at His word — the same drama replayed inside one family in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain," and consummated in "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call."

Symbols defined here:

  • Babel / Babylon = the serpent-seed's confederated city-system: congregation for convenience and self-security in defiance of God's command to fill the earth, and self-naming in defiance of calling on the Name of the LORD; founded by Nimrod on the plain of Shinar, named CONFUSION by God's judgment, and carried forward by the Spirit to "Babylon the great" (Gen. 11:4; Gen. 11:8-9; Gen. 10:8-10; Gen. 9:1; Gen. 4:26; Rev. 17:5).
  • the tower = man-made security against God's judgment and against His command to scatter and fill the earth — brick-and-slime presumption trusted for the safety and the name that belong to the LORD alone, exposed by the LORD's "coming down" and answered by the confusion of tongues and the very scattering it was built to prevent (Gen. 11:3-5; Gen. 11:8).

Symbols carried: the seed of the serpent and the enmity — the God-put division Babel's confederacy tries to erase, mercifully remade by judgment (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"); the city of Cain, calling on the name of the LORD, and the mountains-and-plains geography of the two classes, all resurrected at Shinar (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); the distinction remade by judgment, as at the flood (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); Babel's plain becomes the plain toward which Lot pitches his tent (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"), and Babylon the great receives her final sentence and the last call of separation (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible" and "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

For discussion:

  1. Babel says "let us make us a name" (Gen. 11:4) while Seth's line "began... to call upon the name of the LORD" (Gen. 4:26) — the two classes divided by whose name is invoked. Where in your own life or in the church do we build a name for ourselves — reputation, platform, institution, security — where God is asking us to call on His?
  2. The builders congregated "lest we be scattered" (Gen. 11:4) in direct defiance of "replenish the earth" (Gen. 9:1) — safety in numbers, convenience over command. What forms of congregating for convenience look reasonable to us today, and how do we test whether a gathering is unity in God's word or a confederacy against it (Gen. 11:6)?
  3. God's final answer to "lest we be scattered" is "Come out of her, my people" (Rev. 18:4). If God still scatters His people out of the city of confusion before He judges it, what would it mean this week to accept the scattering rather than the tower — to come out in body and in spirit now, while the call is mercy and not yet plague?

¶7. Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain

The two classes divide one family: Abraham, called out of the Babel-lands, dwells in a tent with an altar at every pitch and confesses himself a pilgrim; Lot pitches his tent toward Sodom and drifts from the plain to the gate — same stock, two classes, and the difference is the direction of the tent door.

The call OUT of the city-civilization — Gen. 12:1; Heb. 11:8:

  • Gen. 12:1. "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee" — the covenant people begin with a command to SEPARATE. Abraham is called out of Ur of the Chaldees — the Babel-lands of Mesopotamia where the serpent's seed congregated (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience") — before he is given a promise: separation precedes worship. The witness of the woman's seed repeats here, c. 2000 BC.
  • Heb. 11:8. "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went" — the going out was the act of faith itself: he obeyed with nothing in hand but the word, leaving the established land for a country not yet seen. (The full pilgrim confession of Heb. 11 is gathered below.)
  • MWV2 266.5. Miller: "Abraham was called to go out from the land of his fathers 'into a strange land, not knowing whither he went'... dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise; for he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose Builder and Maker is God... in the midst of idolatrous nations, among whom they sojourned, not one of them lost their faith, or became impure in their worship" — the pioneer reads the call OUT as the standing pattern: God's people kept pure precisely because they dwelt as pilgrims among the idolaters, not as citizens of their cities.

The tent and the altar — worship travels with the pilgrim — Gen. 12:7-8; 13:4, 18:

  • Gen. 12:7-8. "there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him... and pitched his tent... and there he builded an altar unto the LORD, and called upon the name of the LORD" — the pattern set at the first pitch: everywhere the tent goes up, an altar goes up beside it. Abraham "called upon the name of the LORD" — the dividing act of the faithful seed carried straight down from Seth's line (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name").
    • the tent and the altar = the pilgrim life — dwelling loose from the world with worship at the center, portable, needing no city or temple; Abraham builds an altar at every pitch, so his worship travels with him, and he dwells in tents because he looks for the city God builds (Gen. 12:7-8; Gen. 13:4, 18; Heb. 11:9-10; John 4:23-24). Defined in full at the close.
  • Gen. 13:4. "Unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first: and there Abram called on the name of the LORD" — returning from Egypt, Abraham goes first to the ALTAR, not to a market. Worship, not gain, is the center of his camp.
  • Gen. 13:18. "Then Abram removed his tent, and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron, and built there an altar unto the LORD" — tent removed, altar rebuilt: the whole life is portable worship. The tent moves; the altar always goes up. Abraham too can dwell in a plain — the contrast here is not topography but the altar and the tent-door's direction: Mamre gets an altar; Sodom's plain never does.
  • PP 132.1. White: "Lot was still with him, and again they came to Bethel, and pitched their tents by the altar which they had before erected... Although the whole land had been given him by God Himself, he courteously waived this right" — confirms the tent-and-altar pattern of Gen. 13:3-4, and the pilgrim's non-grasping spirit: Abraham holds so loosely that he waives even God-given rights.

Worship DE-localized — the portable altar validated — John 4:21-24:

  • John 4:21. "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father" — Christ Himself unbinds worship from place: NEITHER this mountain NOR Jerusalem. The city temple was always provisional — a shadow serving its appointed hour; the pilgrim's portable altar anticipated the worship in spirit and truth that Christ here unbinds from every address.
  • John 4:23-24. "the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" — worship is bound to SPIRIT and TRUTH, not to an address. This is why Abraham could worship at every pitch of the tent: the woman's seed never needed the serpent-seed's city to find God.
  • CE 74.1. White: "The Teacher from heaven, no less a personage than the Son of God, came to earth to reveal the character of the Father to men, that they might worship him in spirit and in truth" — confirms the "spirit and truth" definition of true worship; the de-localizing word itself (John 4:21) the Scripture carries alone, as it is fully able to do.

Lot's choice by SIGHT — the well-watered plain — Gen. 13:10-13:

  • Gen. 13:10-12. "And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where... even as the garden of the LORD... Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan... and pitched his tent toward Sodom" — the choice by SIGHT: Lot "lifted up his eyes" and chose what looked like Eden — "as the garden of the LORD" — and no altar is named in his choosing. The tent door now faces the doomed city; the drift begins with a direction.
    • the plain of Sodom = choice by sight — the well-watered convenience, "as the garden of the LORD," chosen with the eyes and no altar named; it ends inside the doomed city, for "toward Sodom" becomes "dwelt in Sodom" becomes "sat in the gate of Sodom" (Gen. 13:10-13; Gen. 14:12; Gen. 19:1). The same eye-led choosing that mingled the sons of God before the flood — "saw... that they were fair... of all which they chose" (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"). Defined in full at the close.
  • Gen. 13:13. "But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly" — Scripture names the corruption in the same breath as the convenience: what looked like the garden of the LORD was a condemned city. The well-watered plain and the exceeding wickedness are one address.
  • PP 133.1. White: "Dazzled with visions of worldly gain, Lot overlooked the moral and spiritual evils that would be encountered there. The inhabitants of the plain were 'sinners before the Lord exceedingly;' but of this he was ignorant, or, knowing, gave it but little weight. He 'chose him all the plain of Jordan,' and 'pitched his tent toward Sodom.' How little did he foresee the terrible results of that selfish choice!" — confirms the symbol exactly: the choice was by sight of worldly gain, and the city's named corruption was weighed as nothing.
  • 1MCP 339.1. White: "Lot chose Sodom as a place of residence because he looked more to the temporal advantages he would gain than to the moral influences that would surround himself and his family... his possessions were destroyed, part of his children perished in the destruction of that wicked city, his wife was turned to a pillar of salt by the way, and he himself was saved 'so as by fire'" — the full harvest of the sight-choice tallied in one sentence: goods, children, wife — everything but the bare soul.

The drift — from "toward" to "dwelt" to "sat in the gate" — Gen. 14:12; 19:1:

  • Gen. 14:12. "And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed" — the tent-door direction has become a street address: "pitched his tent TOWARD Sodom" (Gen. 13:12) is now "DWELT IN Sodom" — and already the city's wars sweep him and his goods away.
  • Gen. 19:1. "And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom" — the final stage: the gate is the seat of the magistrate. Lot is now an officer of the city he once merely faced. Toward, in, gate — one unbroken drift, and not one altar named on the whole road.
  • CL 7.1. White: "Lot trod the plain with unwilling and tardy steps. He had so long associated with evil workers that he could not see his peril until his wife stood on the plain a pillar of salt forever" — confirms the drift's blinding power: long mingling with Sodom dulled the very sense that should have fled it.

The powerless witness and the divided heart — Gen. 19:14, 26; 2 Pet. 2:7-8; Luke 17:32:

  • Gen. 19:14. "Up, get you out of this place; for the LORD will destroy this city. But he seemed as one that mocked unto his sons in law" — the wages of the mingled life: when the hour comes to bear the come-out message, Lot's testimony is powerless. "As one that mocked" — a witness who lived in Sodom's gate cannot be believed against Sodom, even by his own family.
  • 2 Pet. 2:7-8. "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)" — the Spirit's verdict guards the point: Lot was GENUINELY righteous. He is not the serpent's seed; he is the woman's seed lodged in the serpent-seed's city — "vexed... from day to day," saved himself, and losing everything else. The two classes are not decided by pedigree but by where the tent door points.
  • Gen. 19:26. "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt" — her body left Sodom; her heart never did. The backward look monumentalizes the divided soul: half out of the city is still in it. The plain kept what the plain had won.
  • Luke 17:32. "Remember Lot's wife." — Christ distills the whole section into three words and nails them to the end of the age: the peril of the divided heart at the very moment of deliverance. The last generation is commanded to carry this witness (taken up in "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling").
  • PP 169.2. White: "Those who secure for their children worldly wealth and honor at the expense of their eternal interests, will find in the end that these advantages are a terrible loss. Like Lot, many see their children ruined, and barely save their own souls. Their lifework is lost; their life is a sad failure" — confirms 2 Pet. 2:7-8: the righteous soul lodged in the wrong class is saved "so as by fire," and the lifework burns.

The pilgrim confession — strangers seeking a city — Heb. 11:8-10, 13-16; 1 Pet. 2:11:

  • Heb. 11:8. "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went" — the coming out was the act of FAITH: he obeyed before he saw, leaving the established land with nothing in hand but the word.
  • Heb. 11:9-10. "By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles... For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" — the tent explained: Abraham dwells in tabernacles BECAUSE he looks for the city God builds. The tent is a confession about where home is; the pilgrim refuses Cain's city because he is waiting for God's.
  • Heb. 11:13-14. "These all died in faith... and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country" — the confession itself is the mark: to say "strangers and pilgrims" is to "declare plainly" that earth is not home.
    • strangers and pilgrims = the confessed identity of the woman's seed in every age — those who own that earth is not home and openly seek a better, heavenly country; Abraham is the pattern, and the New Testament church wears the same title (Heb. 11:13-16; 1 Pet. 2:11; Gen. 12:1). Defined in full at the close.
  • Heb. 11:15-16. "if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned. But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city" — the road back to Ur stayed open; the pilgrim's not-returning is a daily choice. And the reward is exact: for those who refuse man's city, "he hath prepared for them a CITY."
  • 1 Pet. 2:11. "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul" — the church of the last days inherits Abraham's title verbatim: "strangers and pilgrims" is not patriarchal nostalgia but the standing self-understanding of the woman's seed.
  • PP 169.3. White: "The heritage that God has promised to His people is not in this world. Abraham had no possession in the earth, 'no, not so much as to set his foot on.' Acts 7:5. He possessed great substance, and he used it to the glory of God and the good of his fellow men; but he did not look upon this world as his home" — confirms Heb. 11:9-13: the pilgrim may hold great substance, but he holds it loosely; possession without citizenship.
  • PREX1 24.2. Litch: "It is the city for which the patriarch Abraham looked, (Hebrews 11:10,) 'which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.' For this city he looked as the promised inheritance of the land of Canaan" — the pioneer names the pilgrim's looked-for city: the New Jerusalem, the true inheritance behind the Canaan promise.
  • AA 522.1. White: "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul; having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation" — in AA 522.1 White plants this very text at the head of her charge to the church: the apostolic charter carried forward verbatim.

DEFINITION — ABRAHAM AND LOT — THE TENT AND THE PLAIN = the two classes traced through one family, proving the division is drawn by direction, not descent. Abraham is called OUT of the Babel-lands ("Get thee out of thy country," Gen. 12:1) and lives the rest of his life as a tent-dweller with an altar at every pitch (Gen. 12:7-8; 13:4, 18) — the TENT AND THE ALTAR, portable worship needing no city temple, vindicated by Christ's own word that true worship is bound "neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem" but to "spirit and in truth" (John 4:21-24); he dwells in tabernacles because "he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Heb. 11:9-10), and dies confessing himself among the "strangers and pilgrims on the earth" who "desire a better country" (Heb. 11:13-16) — the confession the New Testament church inherits verbatim (1 Pet. 2:11; AA 522.1). Lot, of the same righteous stock (2 Pet. 2:7-8), lifts up his eyes and chooses THE PLAIN OF SODOM by sight — well watered, "as the garden of the LORD," no altar named (Gen. 13:10-12) — though its men were "sinners before the LORD exceedingly" (Gen. 13:13); and the tent door's direction becomes a destiny: "toward Sodom" (Gen. 13:12), "dwelt in Sodom" (Gen. 14:12), "sat in the gate of Sodom" (Gen. 19:1). The harvest is total: a testimony powerless "as one that mocked" (Gen. 19:14), a wife turned to a pillar of salt by the backward look of a divided heart (Gen. 19:26), children and goods consumed, the man himself "vexed from day to day" and saved so as by fire (2 Pet. 2:8; 1MCP 339.1; PP 169.2). Christ seals the witness for the last generation in three words: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). The witnesses repeat because the classes repeat: the pilgrim by the altar, the drifter at the gate — and the difference between them, first and last, is the direction the tent door faces.

Symbols defined here:

  • the tent and the altar = the pilgrim life — dwelling loose from the world with worship at the center, portable, needing no city or temple; an altar at every pitch, because worship is bound to spirit and truth, not to a place, and the tent confesses that home is the city God builds (Gen. 12:7-8; Gen. 13:4, 18; Heb. 11:9-10; John 4:23-24).
  • the plain of Sodom = choice by sight — the well-watered convenience, "as the garden of the LORD," chosen with the eyes and no altar named, ending inside the doomed city by one unbroken drift: toward, in, gate (Gen. 13:10-13; Gen. 14:12; Gen. 19:1).
  • strangers and pilgrims = the confessed identity of the woman's seed in every age — those who own that earth is not home and declare plainly that they seek a better, heavenly country; Abraham the pattern, the church the heir of the title (Heb. 11:13-16; 1 Pet. 2:11; Gen. 12:1).

Symbols carried: the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent, the two classes this family divides into (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"); the city of Cain and calling on the name of the LORD — Sodom is the city-congregation full grown, and Abraham's altar-call continues Seth's dividing act (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); Babel / Babylon, the city-system of Ur out of which Abraham was called (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"); the mingling and its choice by sight — Lot's eye-led choosing repeats the sons of God who "saw... and took" (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); "Remember Lot's wife" is carried to the last generation in "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling"; the pilgrim's looked-for city and the better country are claimed at last in "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call".

For discussion:

  1. Lot "lifted up his eyes" and chose the plain because it was "well watered every where, even as the garden of the LORD" (Gen. 13:10) — and Scripture names the corruption in the same breath (Gen. 13:13). When you weigh a move, a job, a school, or an alliance, which do you actually weigh first — the water or the wickedness? What would it mean to refuse any choice in which no altar is named?
  2. Lot was "just" and "righteous," yet "vexed his righteous soul from day to day" (2 Pet. 2:7-8), and when the crisis came his warning fell "as one that mocked" (Gen. 19:14). How does a believer's ADDRESS — the class he lodges with — drain the power of his testimony even while his soul remains righteous? Whose warnings in your life have you dismissed for the same reason — and can a vexed soul in the gate of Sodom ever give the come-out call with power?
  3. Abraham dwelt in tents because "he looked for a city which hath foundations" (Heb. 11:10), and the pilgrims "might have had opportunity to have returned" but desired "a better country" (Heb. 11:15-16) — while Lot's wife "looked back" (Gen. 19:26). Since the road back stays open until the end, what does "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32) demand of you this week: which possession, position, or convenience is your own tent door still facing?

¶8. Israel Mingles — "Like All the Nations"

What Balaam's curse could not do from without, his counsel did from within — the daughters, the feast, the strange altar — and the peculiar people finished the work themselves, demanding a king "like all the nations" they were set apart from; the Spirit's post-mortem on the whole national history is one line: "[they] were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works."

The charter of peculiarity — distinctness IS the covenant identity — Exo. 19:5-6; Deut. 14:2; 7:2-6:

  • Exo. 19:5-6. "if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people... And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation" — God's founding charter for the covenant nation: obedience makes Israel His peculiar treasure above all people, a kingdom of priests. Distinctness is not an accessory to the covenant; it IS the covenant identity.
    • peculiar people = God's purchased, set-apart treasure — distinctness is the covenant identity itself, not an ornament upon it; Israel is "a peculiar treasure above all people" and "a kingdom of priests" precisely by keeping the covenant that unlikes them from the nations, and the same charter passes almost word for word to the church redeemed by Christ's blood; to be conformed is to forfeit the identity (Exo. 19:5-6; Deut. 14:2; Deut. 7:6; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:9).
  • Deut. 14:2. "the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations that are upon the earth" — the symbol named in the law itself: chosen TO BE peculiar. The election and the unlikeness are one act.
  • Deut. 7:2-4. "thou shalt make no covenant with them... Neither shalt thou make marriages with them... For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods" — the non-mingling statutes with the reason stated on their face: no covenants, no marriages, because the mingled tie "will turn away thy son." The exact mechanism that dissolved the antediluvian sons of God (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity") is here written into national law.
  • Deut. 7:6. "For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God: the LORD thy God hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth" — the ground of the statute is the identity: because thou ART holy and special, therefore no mingling. The law guards what the election made.

Balaam's forced confession — the appointed posture is dwelling alone — Num. 23:9; Deut. 33:28:

  • Num. 23:9. "lo, the people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations" — Balaam's own hired mouth confesses God's design: the covenant people are appointed to dwell alone, not reckoned among the nations. Separation is the divinely set posture of the woman's seed among the kingdoms.
    • dwelling alone = the appointed posture of the woman's seed among the nations — separation as safety, not isolation as loss; even the prophet hired to curse must confess it, and Moses seals it as shelter, "Israel then shall dwell in safety alone"; the demand for a king "like all the nations" is the deliberate reversal of this posture (Num. 23:9; Deut. 33:28; 1 Sam. 8:5, 20).
  • Deut. 33:28. "Israel then shall dwell in safety alone: the fountain of Jacob shall be upon a land of corn and wine" — Moses' dying blessing frames dwelling alone as SAFETY, not deprivation. The aloneness is the shelter of the peculiar people, joined to fountain, corn, wine, and dew — separation with abundance.
  • PP 439.2. White: "Balaam knew that his curse could not harm Israel. God was on their side, and so long as they were true to Him no adverse power of earth or hell could prevail against them" — the premise of all that follows: no outside curse can touch the people who dwell alone with God. If the enemy is to reach them at all, he must reach them by mingling from within.

The breach at Shittim — what could not be cursed is corrupted — Num. 25:1-3; 31:16; Rev. 2:14:

  • Num. 25:1-2. "the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab. And they called the people unto the sacrifices of their gods: and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods" — the breach at Baal-peor (Shittim, Israel's last camp before Canaan, c. 1407 BC) runs the antediluvian sequence (Gen. 6:2; Matt. 24:38; Gen. 4:3-5): the daughters, the feasts ("did eat"), the false worship ("bowed down"). The mingling mechanism of the old world repeats point for point at the border of the promised land — entering by invitation, not invasion.
  • Num. 25:3. "And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel" — the end of the sequence: the people who could not be cursed are JOINED to Baal-peor by their own act. What Balaam's enchantments could not do, the mingling did.
  • Num. 31:16. "these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to commit trespass against the LORD in the matter of Peor" — Scripture names the author: Baal-peor was not drift but design, "the counsel of Balaam" — the serpent's standing strategy against the peculiar people: corrupt what you cannot curse.
    • the doctrine of Balaam = corrupting by mingling what cannot be cursed — the serpent's standing strategy against the peculiar people; unable to bring a curse from without (Num. 23:9), Balaam counsels Balak to draw Israel into the daughters, the feasts, and the worship of Moab (Num. 25:1-3; Num. 31:16), so that the people curse themselves by their own transgression; Christ names it a permanent doctrine and lays it against a New Testament church (Rev. 2:14).
  • Rev. 2:14. "thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication" — Christ Himself codifies the mechanism as "the doctrine of Balaam" and finds it HELD inside a Christian church. Mingling — the idol feast and the strange marriage — is the enemy's transhistorical method, carried forward to the end (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling").
  • PP 454.2. White: "It was the object of these women, in their association with the Hebrews, to seduce them into transgression of the law of God... These motives were studiously concealed under the garb of friendship" — the breach narrated: the corruption entered "under the garb of friendship," not by open assault. Mingling, not war, is the method.
  • PP 455.1. White: "Their iniquitous practices did that for Israel which all the enchantments of Balaam could not do—they separated them from God" — the doctrine of Balaam stated exactly: the mingling accomplished what the enchantments could not. The curse that heaven refused, the people pronounced upon themselves — and tens of thousands fell by the plague.
  • 4aSG 48.2. White: "there was no way to bring a curse upon them but by seducing them to transgression... He counseled Balak to proclaim an idolatrous feast in honor of their idol gods... and then the most beautiful Midianitish women should entice the Israelites to transgress the law of God... This Satanic counsel succeeded too well" — the counsel of Balaam itemized as a deliberate plan: feast, women, idol sacrifice — the daughters-feasts-worship mechanism in full.
  • DAR 356.1. Smith, on Rev. 2:14: "not being permitted by the Lord to curse them, he resolved to accomplish essentially the same thing, though in a different way. He therefore counseled Balak to seduce them, by means of the females of Moab... The plan succeeded" — the pioneer commentary defining the doctrine of Balaam as corrupting-by-mingling what could not be cursed: the very symbol this section owns.

The vote at Ramah — "make us a king like all the nations" — 1 Sam. 8:5, 7, 19-20:

  • 1 Sam. 8:5. "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations" — c. 1050 BC the peculiar people vote away their peculiarity: the open demand to be reckoned among the very nations Balaam confessed they were set apart from (Num. 23:9). The mingling of Shittim has become a national platform.
  • 1 Sam. 8:7. "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" — God reads the demand for likeness as rejection of His own reign. To want to be like the nations is to unseat the King who made them unlike the nations; the breach is measured at the throne.
  • 1 Sam. 8:19-20. "Nay; but we will have a king over us; That we also may be like all the nations" — the demand doubled and made explicit against Samuel's warning. What the enemy worked by seduction at Peor, the people here choose with open eyes: the peculiar treasure begging to be common coin.
  • GSAM 46.1. Loughborough: "In their dissatisfaction they requested of Samuel that he appoint a king over them, and the Lord said to Samuel, 'They have rejected me, that I should not reign over them'" — the pioneer witness reading the king demand as the rejection of God's reign for likeness to the nations.
  • PP 607.2. White: "God had separated the Israelites from every other people, to make them His own peculiar treasure. But they, disregarding this high honor, eagerly desired to imitate the example of the heathen! And still the longing to conform to worldly practices and customs exists among the professed people of God" — the section's thesis in her own words, tied by her directly to 1 Pet. 2:9: "for the sake of earthly distinction they sacrifice the unspeakable honor" of showing forth His praises. The king demand is the peculiar treasure despising its own peculiarity, and the same conformity-hunger lives on in the modern church.

The crowning case — Solomon and the statute proved true — 1 Kings 11:1-8:

  • 1 Kings 11:1-2. "But king Solomon loved many strange women... Of the nations concerning which the LORD said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall not go in to them... for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods: Solomon clave unto these in love" — c. 930 BC the wisest king breaks the exact marriage statute of Deut. 7:3-4, with the statute's own words quoted over his head as he does it.
  • 1 Kings 11:4. "when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God" — the statute's stated reason proved true to the letter: "they will turn away thy son" — and they turned away the son of David. No wisdom exempts from the law of mingling; the man best equipped to think himself the exception was not.
  • 1 Kings 11:7-8. "Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech... And likewise did he for all his strange wives" — the fruit: the temple-builder erects high places to Chemosh and Molech in the face of the temple itself. Moab's daughters at Shittim, Moab's god above Jerusalem — mingling always ends at the strange altar, the way of Cain rebuilt by the son of David (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships").
  • PK 54.1. White: "Solomon flattered himself that his wisdom and the power of his example would lead his wives from idolatry to the worship of the true God... Vain hope! Solomon's mistake in regarding himself as strong enough to resist the influence of heathen associates was fatal" — the missionary-by-mingling rationalization named and sentenced: alliance does not convert; it corrupts. The world does not rise; the church descends.

The inspired post-mortem — one line over the whole history — Ps. 106:35-36:

  • Ps. 106:35-36. "But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works. And they served their idols: which were a snare unto them" — the Spirit's verdict on the entire national record, from Shittim to the captivity, in one sentence: mingled, learned, served, snared. The two-classes law in four steps — mingling breeds imitation, imitation breeds idolatry, idolatry becomes the snare.
  • 2T 125.1. White: "Many of the professed, peculiar people of God are so conformed to the world that their peculiar character is not discerned, and it is difficult to distinguish 'between him that serveth God and him that serveth Him not'" — the Psalm 106 breach applied to the church: mingling erases the discernible line between the two classes. Distinctness lost is identity lost.

The charter re-issued — the peculiar people carried into the church — Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:9:

  • Titus 2:14. "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works" — the symbol carried forward: Christ's blood purchases "a peculiar people." The set-apart treasure is the redeemed's identity, not an Old Testament relic; the cross re-founds the charter of Sinai.
  • 1 Pet. 2:9. "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness" — the Exo. 19:5-6 charter re-issued to the Christian church almost word for word: chosen, royal priesthood, holy nation, peculiar people. Distinctness remains the covenant identity to the end, and its purpose is witness — "shew forth the praises."
  • AA 521.3. White: "Many of the believers to whom Peter addressed his letters, were living in the midst of heathen, and much depended on their remaining true to the high calling of their profession... 'Ye are a chosen generation... a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people'" — the charter confirmed as a live command to Christians "living in the midst of heathen": the symbol is portable, and the posture it demands is the same.
  • CG 449.3. White: "Our only safety is to stand as God's peculiar people. We must not yield one inch to the customs and fashions of this degenerate age, but stand in moral independence, making no compromise with its corrupt and idolatrous practices" — the peculiar-people symbol defined as SAFETY, the echo of "dwell in safety alone" (Deut. 33:28), and non-mingling — "no compromise" — named as the standing posture of the last church.

DEFINITION — ISRAEL MINGLES — "LIKE ALL THE NATIONS" = the two-classes law applied to the covenant NATION, and proved across its whole history from Shittim (c. 1407 BC) to Samuel (c. 1050 BC) to Solomon (c. 930 BC). God's charter made distinctness the identity itself: obedience to the covenant constitutes Israel "a peculiar treasure... above all people, a kingdom of priests" (Exo. 19:5-6), "a peculiar people... above all the nations" (Deut. 14:2), fenced by non-mingling statutes whose reason is stated on their face — no covenants, no marriages, "for they will turn away thy son from following me" (Deut. 7:2-6). Even Balaam's hired mouth must confess the appointed posture: "the people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations" (Num. 23:9), a dwelling alone that is safety, not loss (Deut. 33:28). And because no curse from without can touch such a people (PP 439.2), the serpent's seed works by its standing method: mingling. At Baal-peor the days-of-Noah sequence repeats — the daughters, the feasts, the bowing down (Num. 25:1-3; Gen. 6:2; Matt. 24:38; Gen. 4:3-5) — by "the counsel of Balaam" (Num. 31:16), accomplishing "that... which all the enchantments of Balaam could not do" (PP 455.1), and Christ codifies the method as "the doctrine of Balaam" still held inside a New Testament church (Rev. 2:14). What entered as seduction matures into policy: "make us a king to judge us like all the nations" (1 Sam. 8:5, 19-20) — the peculiar people voting away their peculiarity, which God weighs at the throne: "they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam. 8:7; PP 607.2; GSAM 46.1). Solomon is the crowning case: the wisest king breaks the exact marriage statute, his wives turn away his heart precisely as the statute foretold, and the temple-builder ends building high places to Chemosh and Molech before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:1-8) — the way of Cain rebuilt by the son of David — the missionary-by-mingling hope pronounced "vain... fatal" (PK 54.1). The Spirit's post-mortem on it all is one line: "[they] were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works... which were a snare unto them" (Ps. 106:35-36). Yet the charter does not die with the nation: Christ redeems and purifies "unto himself a peculiar people" (Titus 2:14), and Peter re-issues Sinai's charter to the church almost word for word (1 Pet. 2:9; AA 521.3), so that "our only safety is to stand as God's peculiar people... making no compromise" (CG 449.3; 2T 125.1). The witness repeats: the mingling that emptied Eden's line before the flood emptied the covenant nation after it — the doctrine of Balaam runs forward into the church's marriage to the empire (see "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith") and waits for the last church (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling," "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible").

Symbols defined here:

  • peculiar people = God's purchased, set-apart treasure — distinctness is not an accessory to the covenant identity, it IS the covenant identity; Israel is a "peculiar treasure above all people" and "a kingdom of priests" precisely by keeping the covenant that unlikes them from the nations, and the same charter passes unchanged to the church redeemed by Christ's blood; to be conformed is to forfeit the identity (Exo. 19:5-6; Deut. 14:2; Deut. 7:6; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:9).
  • dwelling alone = the appointed posture of the woman's seed among the nations — separation as safety, not isolation as loss; Balaam's own mouth confesses the people "shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations," Moses seals it as "dwell in safety alone," and the demand for a king "like all the nations" is the deliberate reversal of the posture (Num. 23:9; Deut. 33:28; 1 Sam. 8:5, 20).
  • the doctrine of Balaam = corrupting by mingling what cannot be cursed — the serpent's standing strategy against the peculiar people; barred from cursing from without, Balaam counsels the daughters, the feasts, and the worship of Moab, so the people curse themselves by their own transgression; Christ names it a permanent doctrine and finds it held in a New Testament church (Num. 31:16; Num. 25:1-3; Num. 23:9; Rev. 2:14).

Symbols carried: the mingling — Baal-peor and Solomon's marriages are the same daughters-feasts-worship mechanism by which the antediluvian sons of God fell (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); the seed of the woman and the enmity — the two classes God set at war, which mingling alone can dissolve (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"); eating and drinking — the idol feast at Peor ("the people did eat") as appetite enlisted against the covenant (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); the strange altar as the terminus of every mingling — Solomon rebuilding the way of Cain (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"); the pilgrim posture Israel abandoned in demanding a throne "like all the nations" (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"); the doctrine of Balaam runs forward into the church's marriage to the empire, the last mingling, and the final separation call (see "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith," "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling," "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

For discussion:

  1. The non-mingling statutes carry their reason on their face — "they will turn away thy son from following me" (Deut. 7:4) — and Solomon, the wisest man, proved them true to the letter when his wives "turned away his heart" (1 Kings 11:4), his convert-them-by-alliance hope pronounced "vain... fatal" (PK 54.1). Where do we run the same "vain hope" today — which alliances do we defend as missionary that Scripture would name as mingling?
  2. Balaam could not curse what God had blessed (Num. 23:9; PP 439.2), so he taught Balak to make Israel curse themselves — daughters, feasts, worship (Num. 25:1-3; Num. 31:16) — and Christ says churches still "hold the doctrine of Balaam" (Rev. 2:14). If no power of earth or hell can prevail against God's people "so long as they were true to Him," what does that make the ONLY door the enemy has into the church — and where is that door standing open among us?
  3. Israel's demand to be "like all the nations" was, in God's own reading, "they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam. 8:7, 19-20), and Ellen White says "still the longing to conform... exists among the professed people of God" (PP 607.2) while "our only safety is to stand as God's peculiar people" (CG 449.3; 1 Pet. 2:9). What specific "king like the nations" — a method, a standard, an ambition borrowed from the world — is your congregation tempted to ask for, and what would "dwelling in safety alone" (Deut. 33:28) look like in its place?

¶9. The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith

The two classes cross into the Christian era unchanged: when the church married the empire, the true church — the woman of Revelation 12 — fled into the wilderness, and for 1260 prophetic days the mountains kept the faith that the mingled majority in the plains and cities had surrendered.

Scripture likens God's people to a woman — the true church defined — Jer. 6:2; Rev. 12:1-2; Eph. 5:25, 27:

  • Jer. 6:2. "I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate [woman]" — Scripture's own key, laid down before the symbol is used: God Himself likens His covenant people, the daughter of Zion, to a woman. The Bible defines its own figure.
  • Rev. 12:1. "And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars" — the woman appears: arrayed in Christ's righteousness, standing on the covenant, crowned with the twelve. She is a corporate body of the faithful, not a city and not a numbers-majority.
    • the woman = the true church, the seed of the woman corporate — the pure bride of Christ, kept distinct by loyalty, not by numbers; God's own likeness for the daughter of Zion (Jer. 6:2; Rev. 12:1-2; Eph. 5:25, 27; Rev. 12:17).
  • Rev. 12:2. "And she being with child cried, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered" — the true church bears Christ into the world through suffering; her identity is a birthing loyalty, not comfort or crowds. She is the woman of the enmity — the seed-bearing line of Genesis 3:15 traced from "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall."
  • Eph. 5:25. "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" — the church is Christ's bride, the pure woman; this is why Scripture figures apostasy as adultery — the woman who marries another has forsaken her true Husband.
  • Eph. 5:27. "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" — the true woman is defined by purity kept, not popularity gained: "not having spot" — the exact opposite of the mingled majority.

Two women, two classes — the bride and the harlot — Rev. 17:5; James 4:4; COL 283.3:

  • Rev. 17:5. "And upon her forehead [was] a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH" — the counter-woman. Prophecy sets two women over against each other: the faithful bride, and the harlot who DID marry the world — Babylon, the city-system of "Babel — Congregating for Convenience" wearing a woman's name. Two women, two classes; there is no third.
  • James 4:4. "Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God" — the great mingling named in one line: a church seeking the friendship of the world commits spiritual adultery. This is the exact mechanism of the fourth-century union.
  • COL 283.3. White: "There are only two classes in the world today, and only two classes will be recognized in the judgment—those who violate God's law and those who obey it. Christ gives the test by which to prove our loyalty or disloyalty" — the two-classes doctrine in bare form: the line runs on obedience to God's commandments, exactly the mark of the woman's remnant seed (Rev. 12:17).

The great mingling repeats — the church marries the empire — GC 43.1; GC 45.1; PP 81.2:

  • GC 43.1. White: "Most of the Christians at last consented to lower their standard, and a union was formed between Christianity and paganism... the Christian religion became corrupted, and the church lost her purity and power. There were some, however, who were not misled by these delusions" — the historical fact: under Constantine the "converted" pagan masses brought their customs in, and the church that stopped fleeing the world lost her purity — while a faithful few refused, splitting the two classes again.
  • GC 45.1. White: "But there is no union between the Prince of light and the prince of darkness, and there can be no union between their followers... He then brought his power to bear more fully upon these, and inspired them to persecute those who remained true to God" — the union of convenience turns persecuting: Satan, having led the compromised church further from truth, "inspired them to persecute those who remained true to God." This is precisely what drives the woman to flee.
  • PP 81.2. White: "For some time the two classes remained separate. The race of Cain... dispersed over the plains and valleys where the children of Seth had dwelt; and the latter, in order to escape from their contaminating influence, withdrew to the mountains... So long as this separation continued, they maintained the worship of God in its purity. But in the lapse of time they ventured, little by little, to mingle with the inhabitants of the valleys" — the master pattern from before the flood (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"): Cain's race in the plains, the faithful in the mountains, worship kept pure only while separate. The Christian era now repeats it point for point.

The woman flees — the wilderness and the 1260 days — Rev. 12:6, 14; MWM 213.1:

  • Rev. 12:6. "And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred [and] threescore days" — the section's title text. When the empire married the church, the true church did not conquer the plains — she FLED, kept distinct by separation, fed by God in a place He prepared, for the 1260 prophetic days.
    • the wilderness = the place of preservation-by-separation for the true church during the mingled centuries — not a geography but a condition: God's provided refuge, entered by flight rather than conquest, where the woman is fed away from the serpent through the 1260 days/years (Rev. 12:6; Rev. 12:14; Heb. 11:38; 2 Cor. 6:17).
  • Rev. 12:14. "And to the woman were given two wings of a great eagle, that she might fly into the wilderness, into her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent" — the flight restated: God's own provision (eagle's wings, cf. Ex. 19:4) carries the church into HER place, nourished away from the serpent for time + times + half a time — the same 1260, the medieval night.
  • MWM 213.1. Miller: "Three times we have witnessed... the fulfilment of the 'time, times, and an half,' in the accomplishment of the 'forty-two months,' in the completion of the 'twelve hundred and three-score days'" — the pioneer reading: time, times, and a half = forty-two months = 1260 days, one period, its fulfilment already witnessed.

The mountains keep the faith — Heb. 11:37-38; GC 64.1; 65.2-3; 267.2:

  • Heb. 11:37. "They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented" — the roll of the faithful reaches the persecuted witnesses: the same class as the wilderness woman, marked by loss for the truth's sake.
  • Heb. 11:38. "(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and [in] mountains, and [in] dens and caves of the earth" — the faith chapter's roll of the persecuted ends here: "in deserts, and in mountains." And the verdict is inverted from all appearance — the mingled majority that held the cities and called itself the church was the world "not worthy" of the exiles it hunted. The mountain-and-plain geography of the two classes holds (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name").
  • GC 64.1. White: "There were some, however, who refused to yield to the authority of pope or prelate... A separation took place. Those who adhered to the ancient faith now withdrew... others retreated to the secluded glens and rocky fastnesses of the mountains, and there preserved their freedom to worship God" — PP 81 replayed point for point: "A separation took place," and the faithful "retreated... to the mountains" — the Waldenses, the wilderness woman in the flesh.
  • GC 65.2. White: "They declared the Church of Rome to be the apostate Babylon of the Apocalypse... Through ages of darkness and apostasy there were Waldenses who denied the supremacy of Rome, who rejected image worship as idolatry, and who kept the true Sabbath" — the mountain church stands opposite the counter-woman of Rev. 17:5: they named Rome the apostate Babylon, and their mark was obedience — the true Sabbath kept — the same commandment-line that runs to "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible."
  • GC 65.3. White: "Behind the lofty bulwarks of the mountains—in all ages the refuge of the persecuted and oppressed—the Waldenses found a hiding place. Here the light of truth was kept burning amid the darkness of the Middle Ages. Here, for a thousand years, witnesses for the truth maintained the ancient faith" — the mountains as the wilderness refuge, truth "kept burning" through the medieval night. (The "thousand years" is the round historical span of the Middle Ages; the precise prophetic measure is the 1260 of Rev. 12:6, 14.)
  • GC 267.2. White: "God's witnesses remained in a state of obscurity... hunted, betrayed, tortured, buried in dungeon cells, martyred for their faith, or compelled to flee to mountain fastnesses, and to dens and caves of the earth—then the faithful witnesses prophesied in sackcloth. Yet they continued their testimony throughout the entire period of 1260 years" — the direct bridge from text to history: the witnesses driven to "dens and caves of the earth" (Heb. 11:38 verbatim) through the 1260 years — the wilderness woman and the sackcloth witnesses are one company.

No cathedral — worship in spirit and in truth — John 4:21, 23-24; GC 66.1-2:

  • John 4:21. "Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father" — Christ DE-localizes worship: it is bound to no city, no temple, no shrine. The point is not that mountains are the appointed place of worship — it is that worship is freed from place entirely, so the wilderness church needs no cathedral.
  • John 4:23. "But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him" — the true worshippers carry a portable altar — the pilgrim worship of Abraham's tent-altars in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain" — and this is exactly how the woman worships in the wilderness: no building, full acceptance with God.
  • John 4:24. "God [is] a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship [him] in spirit and in truth" — the definition of acceptable worship is inward loyalty, not architecture: the ground for reading the wilderness centuries as genuine, God-accepted worship.
  • GC 66.1. White: "God had provided for His people a sanctuary of awful grandeur, befitting the mighty truths committed to their trust. To those faithful exiles the mountains were an emblem of the immutable righteousness of Jehovah... God's servants should be as firm as the unchanging hills" — no cathedral, and none needed: God's own provision was their sanctuary, and the mountains preached His law's immutability to those who kept it.
  • GC 66.2. White: "They thanked God that He had provided for them an asylum from the wrath and cruelty of men. They rejoiced in their freedom to worship before Him...
