From many a lofty cliff they chanted the praise of God, and the armies of Rome could not silence their songs of thanksgiving" — the "place prepared of God" of Rev. 12:6 realized: an asylum from the dragon's wrath where the woman worships freely, in spirit and in truth.

Separation is the standing command — the line runs to the remnant — 2 Cor. 6:17-18; Rev. 12:17; 18:4; MWM 316.2:

  • 2 Cor. 6:17. "Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean [thing]; and I will receive you" — the command that defines the class in every age: SEPARATION. The wilderness flight is this imperative obeyed under persecution.
  • 2 Cor. 6:18. "And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty" — the reward of separation is sonship: the place "prepared of God" is where He receives and fathers those who came out.
  • MWM 316.2. Miller: "A church, according to the Scriptures, is a religious assembly, selected and called out of the world, by the doctrine of the gospel, to worship the true God according to his word... we have... 'the church in the wilderness,' Acts 7:38" — the pioneer definition: the church is by nature CALLED OUT of the world; "the church in the wilderness" is one of Scripture's own names for her.
  • Rev. 12:17. "And the dragon was wroth with the woman, and went to make war with the remnant of her seed, which keep the commandments of God, and have the testimony of Jesus Christ" — the wilderness woman is one continuous line ending in a commandment-keeping remnant. The mark of the true class is never numbers but obedience and testimony — the seed of the woman of "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall," carried forward to "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible."
  • Rev. 18:4. "And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues" — the same come-out call re-sounded at the end. The wilderness principle is not medieval-only: it is the standing summons out of the church-world union, from Constantine's day to the final call of "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call."

DEFINITION — THE CHURCH IN THE WILDERNESS — THE MOUNTAINS KEEP THE FAITH = the two classes cross into the Christian era unchanged. The true church is the woman — Scripture's own likeness for the daughter of Zion (Jer. 6:2), the pure bride Christ loved and will present "not having spot" (Eph. 5:25, 27), clothed with the sun and travailing to bear Christ to the world (Rev. 12:1-2) — and her counterfeit is the harlot Babylon who married the world (Rev. 17:5), for "the friendship of the world is enmity with God" (James 4:4). When the fourth-century church consented to a "union... between Christianity and paganism" and "lost her purity and power" (GC 43.1), the mingling of Genesis 6 repeated inside the church, and Satan inspired the compromised body to persecute those who remained true to God (GC 45.1); so the woman FLED into the wilderness, to "a place prepared of God," fed and nourished on eagle's wings away from the serpent for the 1260 days — a time, times, and half a time, the forty-two months, one period (Rev. 12:6, 14; MWM 213.1). The wilderness is a condition, not a shrine: Hebrews locates the faithful "in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth," a class "of whom the world was not worthy" (Heb. 11:37-38), and history fills in the names — the pattern of PP 81 replayed point for point: "a separation took place," and the faithful "retreated... to the mountains" (GC 64.1; PP 81.2) — the Waldenses, who named Rome the apostate Babylon and kept the true Sabbath (GC 65.2), keeping the light burning "behind the lofty bulwarks of the mountains" through the medieval night (GC 65.3), the very words in which the 1260-year witnesses prophesied in sackcloth (GC 267.2). Their worship needed no cathedral, for Christ had freed worship from every place — "neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem," but "in spirit and in truth" (John 4:21-24) — and God Himself provided their sanctuary and asylum (GC 66.1-2). The abiding law of the class is "come out from among them, and be ye separate" answered by sonship (2 Cor. 6:17-18; MWM 316.2), and the wilderness line ends in a remnant "which keep the commandments of God, and have the testimony of Jesus Christ" (Rev. 12:17; COL 283.3) — the same summons still sounding at the end: "Come out of her, my people" (Rev. 18:4). The mingled majority held the cities and the name, and called itself the church; the mountains kept the faith.

Symbols defined here:

  • the woman = the true church, the seed of the woman corporate — the pure bride of Christ, kept distinct by loyalty rather than numbers; God likens the daughter of Zion to a woman, Christ loves the church as a husband his wife "not having spot," and her remnant seed keep the commandments of God and the testimony of Jesus, over against the harlot Babylon who married the world (Jer. 6:2; Rev. 12:1-2, 17; Eph. 5:25, 27; Rev. 17:5).
  • the wilderness = the place of preservation-by-separation for the true church during the mingled centuries — a condition, not a geography: God's provided refuge, entered by flight and not conquest, where the woman is fed away from the serpent through the 1260 days/years; needing no cathedral because worship is "in spirit and in truth," and located by Scripture itself "in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth" (Rev. 12:6, 14; Heb. 11:38; John 4:23-24; 2 Cor. 6:17).

Symbols carried: the enmity and the two seeds, the God-put division this section traces through the Christian era (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"); mountains and plains, the geography of the two classes that the Waldenses repeat point for point (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); the mingling, the church-marries-empire mechanism of the fourth-century fall (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); Babel / Babylon, the city-system the harlot of Rev. 17:5 names on her forehead (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"); the tent and the altar and pilgrims and strangers, the portable in-spirit-and-truth worship the mountain church inherited (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"); the peculiar people and dwelling alone, the covenant identity the wilderness preserved (see "Israel Mingles — "Like All the Nations""); the commandments-and-faith remnant of Rev. 12:17, drawn out to its final visible form (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible"); the come-out call of Rev. 18:4, sounded in full at the close (see "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

For discussion:

  1. The woman's mark is never numbers: she flees while the majority holds the cities and the name, and Scripture says the world "was not worthy" of the wanderers in the mountains (Rev. 12:6; Heb. 11:38). Where do we still measure the true church — or our own standing — by size, visibility, or institutional standing, and what would it change to measure by Rev. 12:17's two marks, the commandments of God and the testimony of Jesus?
  2. The church fell not by persecution but by friendship: "a union was formed between Christianity and paganism" when the standard was lowered (GC 43.1), and "the friendship of the world is enmity with God" (James 4:4). What "half-converted" customs and alliances press on the church now, and how do we refuse the union without refusing the people?
  3. Christ freed worship from every place: "neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem... in spirit and in truth" (John 4:21, 23) — so the Waldenses worshiped fully accepted with no cathedral (GC 66.1-2). What would it change this week if your acceptance with God rested wholly on inward loyalty rather than on place, building, or crowd — and what "portable altar" would that require you to carry?

Part IV — The Days of the Son of Man

¶10. As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling

Christ appointed BOTH Genesis judgments — the flood and Sodom — as one picture of the last age: lawful things made the whole of life, the covenant line mingled with the world until "knew not," and sudden separation by judgment "the same day" the righteous go out; the last mingling is not out in the world but inside the church, and against it the old calls of separation sound again as present truth.

Christ appoints the FIRST Genesis judgment as the picture of the last age — Luke 17:26-27; Matt. 24:37-39:

  • Luke 17:26. "And as it was in the days of Noe, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man" — Christ Himself fixes the type: the antediluvian world is the mirror of the last generation. He does not reach for a new figure; He reaches back to the first judgment.
    • the days of the Son of man = the last age, defined by Christ Himself through the matched Noah/Lot pattern — heedless absorption in lawful things ("they did eat, they drank... bought... sold... planted... builded"), mingled worship as the covenant line blends with the world, and sudden separation by judgment on "the same day" the righteous go out; the mark is not open rebellion but "knew not" (Luke 17:26-30; Matt. 24:37-39; Gen. 6:2, 5; Gen. 13:12-13). Defined in full at the close.
  • Luke 17:27. "They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all" — four verbs, every one lawful. Eating, drinking, and marrying made the whole of life right up to the day of separation; not one open crime is named — the indictment is absorption.
  • Matt. 24:37. "But as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be." — the parallel account fixes the same appointment; the days of Noah are not an illustration but a stated equivalence.
  • Matt. 24:38-39. "they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage... And knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" — the diagnosis in two words: "knew not." Heedlessness, not defiance, is the mark of the age (eating and drinking as the mark of the heedless class is defined in "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack").
  • DA 633.1. White: "Christ continues, pointing out the condition of the world at His coming: 'As the days of Noah were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be'... He tells us that as it was in Noah's day, so will it be when the Son of man comes again." — confirms that the Noah saying is Christ's own definition of the state of the world at His coming, not merely its suddenness.
  • AH 121.3. White: "There is in itself no sin in eating and drinking, or in marrying and giving in marriage... But in the days of Noah men married without consulting God..." — the precise edge of the charge: the condemned things were LAWFUL, carried on without God until they became the whole of life.

The SECOND judgment added as a matched pair — the days of Lot — Luke 17:28-30:

  • Luke 17:28. "Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded" — six verbs now: to the antediluvian four Christ adds buying, selling, planting, building — the busy commerce of the city. The last age is pictured as uninterrupted business.
  • Luke 17:29-30. "But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all. Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed" — "the same day": the going out of the righteous and the fall of judgment are one event, as at the ark door. The commerce runs to the very hour.
  • CD 17.6. White: "Our Saviour warned His disciples that just prior to His second coming a state of things would exist very similar to that which preceded the flood. Eating and drinking would be carried to excess... more and more like the doomed inhabitants of Sodom" — joins BOTH judgments, flood and Sodom, as one last-days picture of appetite and pleasure — exactly Luke 17's pairing.
  • CD 435.2. White: "The world's Redeemer, who knows well the state of society in the last days, represents eating and drinking as the sins that condemn this age" — names the lawful-made-ultimate as the condemning sin of the age, per the Noah pattern.

What "the days of Noah" actually were — the mingling behind the meals — Gen. 6:2, 5:

  • Gen. 6:2. "That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose" — behind the eating and marrying stood the MINGLING: the covenant line of Seth blended with the line of Cain, and the distinction dissolved (the sons of God, the daughters of men, and the mingling are defined in "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"). The attack fell on the Eden institution of marriage.
  • Gen. 6:5. "And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" — the result once the two classes blended: universal corruption. The mingling, not merely open sin, produced the world the flood swept away.
  • PP 81.2. White: "For some time the two classes remained separate... So long as this separation continued, they maintained the worship of God in its purity. But in the lapse of time they ventured, little by little, to mingle with the inhabitants of the valleys... and they lost their peculiar, holy character" — the master witness: separation maintained the pure worship, and gradual mingling — "little by little" — dissolved the peculiar character. THIS is the substance of "as it was in the days of Noe."
  • PP 85.4. White: Enoch, "fearing that their infidelity might lessen his reverence for God... avoided constant association with them, and spent much time in solitude, giving himself to meditation and prayer" — the counter-example inside the same generation: deliberate separation from the mingled society preserved the walk with God.

The last mingling is from INSIDE — a form of godliness, Laodicea at ease — 2 Tim. 3:1-5; Rev. 3:17:

  • 2 Tim. 3:1-2. "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous..." — Paul dates the catalogue "in the last days," and the peril is a character-list, not a persecution-list: the danger comes from what men LOVE.
  • 2 Tim. 3:4-5. "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away" — the crisis of the list: these are the PROFESSED. The Noah/Lot mingling is relocated from the world into the church — appetite and pleasure ruling under an exterior of piety — and the command is still separation: "from such turn away."
    • having a form of godliness = the last-days condition inside the church: an outward shape of religion emptied of its power, the professed mingled with the world in appetite and pleasure while keeping the exterior of piety — the Noah/Lot mingling moved from the world into the sanctuary (2 Tim. 3:1-5; Rev. 3:17; Matt. 24:39). Defined in full at the close.
  • Rev. 3:17. "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked" — Laodicea: the church at ease in the city, and — like the antediluvians — "knowest not." The days-of-Noah heedlessness has entered the sanctuary.
  • COL 158.3. White: "The Lord says, 'Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing...' The gold tried in the fire is faith that works by love" — applies Rev. 3:17 to the church's self-satisfied wealth; the remedy is not more goods but tried faith.
  • MYP 390.2. White: "The eternal God has drawn the line of distinction between the saint and the sinner... The two classes do not blend into each other imperceptibly, like the colors of a rainbow, but are as distinct as midday and midnight" — carries the two-classes line into the end time, and names the modern mingling precisely: "God's people cannot with safety enter into intimate associations with those who know the truth, but do not practice it."

Against it, the old calls sound again — out of the cities — Gen. 13:12-13; CH 268.1:

  • Gen. 13:12-13. "Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom. But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly" — the two-classes divergence in one verse: Abraham in the pilgrim land, Lot drifting cityward while the city's wickedness is named in the same breath (the tent-and-altar life and the plain of Sodom are defined in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain").
  • PP 168.1. White: "In how wide contrast to the life of Abraham was that of Lot! Once they had been companions, worshiping at one altar... Lot had chosen Sodom for its pleasure and profit... he had permitted his children to mingle with a corrupt and idolatrous people" — the narrative of the drift: one altar shared, then the city chosen for pleasure and profit, and the children lost to mingling.
  • CH 268.1. White: "'Out of the cities,' is my message... I hope and pray and believe that they will now arouse to the importance of getting out into the country" — the present-truth reissue of the old separations: her repeated turn-of-the-century "Out of the cities" appeals reissued the antediluvian separation as present truth for the last generation — the modern tent-pitching.
  • CL 5.2. White: "Parents flock with their families to the cities, because they fancy it easier to obtain a livelihood there... they stay where they are, until Satan gains full control of their children" — the modern Lot-toward-Sodom drift named: cityward for livelihood, exactly as Lot chose the plain, and the children lost to the mingling exactly as in Sodom.
  • John 4:21, 23-24. "neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem... the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth... God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" — the call out of the city costs no worship: Christ de-localizes it. The peculiar people are bound to no city or temple; they carry the true worship with them, as Abraham carried his altar.

The return toward the Eden table — Gen. 1:29:

  • Gen. 1:29. "Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat" — the original grant, one of the institutions of Eden with marriage and the Sabbath (the institutions of Eden and the original diet are defined in "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); flesh was not granted until after the flood (Gen. 9:3).
  • Ev 663.4. White: "In the beginning, fruit was pronounced by God as 'good for food.' The permission to eat flesh meat was a consequence of the fall. Not till after the Flood was man given permission to eat the flesh of animals" — anchors the health message to Genesis: Gen. 1:29 the original table, flesh a post-fall, post-flood concession.
  • CG 383.1. White: "Is it not time that all should aim to dispense with flesh foods?... Let them, rather, return to the wholesome and delicious food given to man in the beginning" — the reform framed explicitly as a RETURN toward Eden's institution: not salvation by menu, but the peculiar people re-learning the institutions of Eden while the world perfects the way of Cain (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships").

The last-generation text — Remember Lot's wife — Luke 17:32; Gen. 19:26:

  • Luke 17:32. "Remember Lot's wife." — three words, Christ's own memorial nailed into the days-of-the-Son-of-man discourse itself. The warning is not against staying in the city; she had left it. It is against a divided leaving of it — a separation of the feet without a separation of the heart.
    • Remember Lot's wife = the last-generation warning against a divided separation — out of the city with the body, in it with the heart; she obeyed the call to come out, and one backward look fixed her forever as the standing type of the professor whose separation never reached the affections (Luke 17:32; Gen. 19:26; Gen. 13:12-13). Defined in full at the close.
  • Gen. 19:26. "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt" — the literal fate the command points back to: her feet left Sodom, her heart lingered, and the lingering look was fatal. Separation of the body without separation of the heart is no separation at all.

DEFINITION — AS IN THE DAYS OF NOAH — THE LAST MINGLING = Christ appointed both Genesis judgments as one picture of the last age: "as it was in the days of Noe... likewise also as it was in the days of Lot" (Luke 17:26-30; Matt. 24:37-39) — lawful things made the whole of life ("they did eat, they drank, they married wives... they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded"), carried on "until the day" the righteous went out and judgment fell "the same day," with the fatal diagnosis "knew not." Behind the antediluvian meals and marriages stood the mingling: the sons of God took the daughters of men (Gen. 6:2), the two classes blended, "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen. 6:5) — for "so long as this separation continued, they maintained the worship of God in its purity," and mingling "little by little" cost them their "peculiar, holy character" (PP 81.2). The last generation meets this same mingling from INSIDE the profession: "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof" (2 Tim. 3:1-5), Laodicea "rich, and increased with goods... and knowest not" (Rev. 3:17) — the church at ease in the city, distinct from the world "as midday and midnight" in God's intent (MYP 390.2) yet blending in fact. Against it the old calls of Eden and of Abraham sound again as present truth: "'Out of the cities,' is my message" (CH 268.1; CL 5.2) — the modern tent-pitching against the modern drift toward the plain (Gen. 13:12-13; PP 168.1) — and the return toward the Eden table of Gen. 1:29 (Ev 663.4; CG 383.1), the peculiar people re-learning the institutions of Eden while the world perfects the way of Cain, carrying worship "in spirit and in truth" out of every city (John 4:21-24). And over the whole age stands Christ's shortest sermon: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32; Gen. 19:26) — for the days of the Son of man end as Noah's and Lot's did, in sudden separation by judgment, and the only separation that survives it is one of the heart. The two classes here re-formed become fully and finally visible in the seal and the mark (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible"), under the last form of the old call: "Come out of her, my people" (see "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

Symbols defined here:

  • the days of the Son of man = the last age, defined by Christ through the matched Noah/Lot pattern — heedless absorption in lawful things (eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building), mingled worship as the covenant line blends with the world, and sudden separation by judgment on "the same day" the righteous go out; the mark of the age is "knew not" (Luke 17:26-30; Matt. 24:37-39; Gen. 6:2, 5; Gen. 13:12-13).
  • Remember Lot's wife = the last-generation warning against a divided separation — out of the city with the body, in it with the heart; she obeyed the call to come out, and one backward look fixed her forever as the standing type of the professor whose separation never reached the affections (Luke 17:32; Gen. 19:26; Gen. 13:12-13).
  • having a form of godliness = the last-days condition inside the church: an outward shape of religion emptied of its power, the professed mingled with the world in appetite and pleasure while keeping the exterior of piety — the Noah/Lot mingling relocated from the world into the sanctuary, Laodicea "rich, and increased with goods" yet "knowest not" (2 Tim. 3:1-5; Rev. 3:17; Matt. 24:39).

Symbols carried: the mingling, the sons of God, and the daughters of men — the mechanism by which the peculiar people lose their peculiarity (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); the institutions of Eden, the original diet, and eating and drinking as the mark of the heedless class (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); the tent and the altar, the plain of Sodom, and the pilgrim identity behind the out-of-the-cities call (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"); the peculiar people (see "Israel Mingles — 'Like All the Nations'"); the way of Cain, the self-chosen worship the world perfects while the remnant returns to the appointed way (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"); the two classes made finally visible in seal and mark (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible"); and the last call out of the city (see "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

For discussion:

  1. Every verb in Christ's picture of the last age is lawful — "they did eat, they drank... they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded" (Luke 17:27-28) — and the fatal word is "knew not" (Matt. 24:39). Where in your own life has a lawful thing quietly become the whole of life — and how would you find out, given that the very mark of this condition is not knowing?
  2. Paul locates the last mingling inside the profession — "a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof" (2 Tim. 3:5) — and Laodicea says "I am rich... and knowest not" (Rev. 3:17), while PP 81.2 says the two classes were safe only "so long as this separation continued" and fell "little by little." What does the Sethites' little-by-little descent to the valleys look like among us now — in associations, in appetite, in what we love (MYP 390.2)?
  3. "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32): she was already out of Sodom in body when the look destroyed her (Gen. 19:26). If the calls out of the city and back toward the Eden table (CH 268.1; Gen. 1:29) were obeyed only in address and menu, what would be gained? What would a separation of the heart — not merely of the feet — look like for you this week?

¶11. The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible

The war on appointed worship that opened at Cain's altar terminates at the Sabbath: the two classes reach their final, universal, visible form — all the world marked for the beast's self-appointed worship, or sealed in the forehead with the sign of Him that made heaven and earth — and judgment makes the distinction permanent.

The war on worship goes universal — Rev. 13:3-4:

  • Rev. 13:3. "his deadly wound was healed: and all the world wondered after the beast" — the power whose fourth-century church-world union supplanted the Creator's appointed day (the union traced in "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith"; GC chs. 3-4) recovers its dominion, and the wondering is now worldwide. The two classes are about to become visible on a world scale.
  • Rev. 13:4. "they worshipped the dragon which gave power unto the beast: and they worshipped the beast, saying, Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him?" — the text names the issue itself: WORSHIP. The serpent's seed does not end in mere irreligion but in a rival worship, dragon-empowered, universal — the enmity of the two seeds (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall") fought out at the last altar.

The mark enforced — and the siege of buying and selling — Rev. 13:16-17:

  • Rev. 13:16. "he causeth all, both small and great, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads" — the rival worship is ENFORCED on every class of men; the badge of allegiance is set where choice lives (the forehead) or where conduct complies (the hand).
    • the mark of the beast = allegiance to the self-appointed worship-system enforced in place of the Creator's appointed worship — the way of Cain full grown, the substitute offering (Gen. 4:3-5) become world law; received in forehead or hand (Rev. 13:16), set opposite "the commandments of God" (Rev. 14:9-12), and enforced by economic siege (Rev. 13:17). Defined in full at the close.
  • Rev. 13:17. "that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name" — the city-system's final weapon against the separate class: the confederated commerce of Babel turned into a siege engine (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"; see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"). Cain's congregation no longer merely excludes the separate; it starves them. The pilgrims (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain") are pressed toward conformity.
  • CS 59.3. White: "The time is coming when we cannot sell at any price. The decree will soon go forth prohibiting men to buy or sell of any man save he that hath the mark of the beast" — confirms Rev. 13:17 as a literal, coming decree against the class that will not conform.

The first angel answers — worship Him that MADE — Rev. 14:6-7; Exo. 20:8-11; Gen. 2:1-3:

  • Rev. 14:7. "Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come: and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters" — heaven's counter-summons: worship the CREATOR. The phrase is lifted from the fourth commandment; the angel answers the beast's worship by pointing all the world back to the Creator's own memorial.
  • Exo. 20:8, 10. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy... the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God" — the commandment the first angel echoes; the day is the LORD'S, not man's to appoint.
  • Exo. 20:11. "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is... wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it" — the exact ground Rev. 14:7 stands on: "made heaven, and earth, and the sea." To worship Him that made is to keep the memorial He appointed for the making.
  • Gen. 2:3. "And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made" — the Sabbath instituted in Eden, before any fall or any nation — one of the three institutions of Eden the serpent's seed has warred on from the beginning (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"). The end-time battle over worship is a fight over the original, appointed day.
  • CCh 334.6. White: "The Sabbath question is to be the issue in the great final conflict in which all the world will act a part... Each sabbath institution bears the name of its author, an ineffaceable mark that shows the authority of each" — each day carries its author's authority: the Creator's appointed Sabbath against the self-chosen day — Abel's appointed offering against Cain's substitute, on a world scale (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships").

God names the Sabbath His SIGN — Exo. 31:13-17; Eze. 20:12, 20:

  • Exo. 31:13. "Verily my sabbaths ye shall keep: for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations; that ye may know that I am the LORD that doth sanctify you" — God Himself names the Sabbath His SIGN: the mark of the God who sanctifies, set between Him and His people.
  • Exo. 31:17. "It is a sign... for ever: for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed" — the sign is "for ever," and its content is creation — the same credential the first angel proclaims (Rev. 14:7).
  • Eze. 20:12. "I gave them my sabbaths, to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD that sanctify them" — the sign identifies WHOSE people they are, and that God — not they themselves — sanctifies them.
  • Eze. 20:20. "And hallow my sabbaths; and they shall be a sign between me and you, that ye may know that I am the LORD your God" — the sign marks those who acknowledge the Creator's authority against every rival: the self-appointed system carries the authority of its own maker.

The sign set in the forehead is the seal — Rev. 7:2-3; 14:1; Eze. 9:4-6:

  • Rev. 7:2-3. "having the seal of the living God... Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads" — the judgment winds are held back until the servants of God are sealed in their FOREHEADS. A sign set in the forehead is a seal; the Sabbath-sign of Exo. 31 and Eze. 20 is here fixed on the separate class before the plagues fall.
    • the seal of God = the Creator's sign of ownership and sanctification set in the forehead — the seventh-day Sabbath kept by faith. Scripture calls the Sabbath God's "sign" that He is the LORD who made heaven and earth and who sanctifies His people (Exo. 31:13-17; Eze. 20:12, 20); the sign in the forehead is the seal (Rev. 7:2-3), and the sealed bear the Father's name (Rev. 14:1). Defined in full at the close.
  • Rev. 14:1. "a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand, having his Father's name written in their foreheads" — the sealed bear the Father's NAME — His character and authority — the exact opposite of the beast's name and mark (Rev. 13:17).
  • Eze. 9:4. "set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof" — the Old Testament type of the sealing: its mark — the seal-type — falls on the MOURNERS over abomination, not on the comfortable majority of the professed people.
  • Eze. 9:6. "but come not near any man upon whom is the mark; and begin at my sanctuary" — the slaying spares only the marked, and it begins at the sanctuary: the distinction is drawn inside the professed church first, then made permanent by judgment — the flood-pattern of the two classes repeated (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling").
  • SSP 132.2. Haskell: "this knowledge of God, is the seal placed in the foreheads of the chosen generation... this, Jehovah has placed in His Sabbath... The seal placed in the forehead by the angel, cannot be read by man; only God and heavenly beings can read it. For this reason, no civil law can enforce Sabbath keeping. Man may keep the form one day in seven, but only a knowledge of God can give the seal in the forehead" — the pioneer exposition binding Rev. 7 to the Sabbath-sign of Exo. 31 and Eze. 20: the seal is a knowledge of God, and precisely because it is inward, no decree can counterfeit it — only the mark can be enforced by law.

The third angel names the two classes — Rev. 14:9-12:

  • Rev. 14:9-10. "If any man worship the beast and his image, and receive his mark in his forehead, or in his hand, The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God" — the third angel's warning defines the mark by its object: WORSHIP of the beast and his image — allegiance to the self-appointed system enforced in place of the Creator's appointed worship. The way of Cain (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships") stands full grown: a substitute worship, now persecuting the true.
  • Rev. 14:12. "Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus" — the sealed class named against the mark-bearers: commandment-keepers (the Sabbath memorial included) holding the faith of Jesus — Abel's line in its final, visible form.
  • TMR 112.1. Andrews: "the worship of the beast and his image, and the reception of his mark, is the opposite of keeping the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. And we have seen that one of the commandments of God has been superseded by an institution of the Romish apostasy" — the pioneer statement of the antithesis: the mark is the supplanting of the Sabbath commandment itself.
  • GC 605.2. White: "The Sabbath will be the great test of loyalty... While one class, by accepting the sign of submission to earthly powers, receive the mark of the beast, the other, choosing the token of allegiance to divine authority, receive the seal of God" — the master statement: the Sabbath is the final test that draws the visible line between the two classes.
  • 8T 117.4. White: "The sign, or seal, of God is revealed in the observance of the seventh-day Sabbath, the Lord's memorial of creation.... The mark of the beast is the opposite of this—the observance of the first day of the week. This mark distinguishes those who acknowledge the supremacy of the papal authority from those who acknowledge the authority of God" (compiled in LDE 224.3) — seal = the Creator's memorial; mark = its opposite: the badge distinguishing the two allegiances.
  • Ev 235.2. White: "When you obey the decree that commands you to cease from labor on Sunday and worship God, while you know that there is not a word in the Bible showing Sunday to be other than a common working day, you consent to receive the mark of the beast, and refuse the seal of God" — the mark is received KNOWINGLY: informed submission to the enforced substitute over the Creator's appointed day.
  • SR 383.3. White: "In the issue of the great contest, two distinct, opposite classes are developed. One class 'worship the beast and his image, and receive his mark'... The other class, in marked contrast to the world, 'keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus'" — the two-classes thesis of the whole study stated in its final-conflict form.

The door shuts — the distinction fixed forever — Rev. 22:11:

  • Rev. 22:11. "He that is unjust, let him be unjust still... and he that is holy, let him be holy still" — probation closes and the two classes are fixed forever. As at the flood the LORD shut the door and judgment fixed the separation the mingled world had blurred (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling"), so the distinction made visible by seal and mark is made permanent by judgment. After this word there is no third class and no crossing over.

DEFINITION — THE SEAL OR THE MARK — THE DISTINCTION MADE VISIBLE = the final, universal form of the two classes, drawn at the point of appointed worship. The healed beast carries the war on worship to all the world (Rev. 13:3-4) and enforces a mark — allegiance to a self-appointed worship-system, the way of Cain full grown — on forehead and hand, with an economic siege against all who refuse (Rev. 13:16-17). Heaven answers by the first angel's summons to "worship him that made heaven, and earth" (Rev. 14:7), the very language of the fourth commandment (Exo. 20:8-11), pointing to the memorial planted in Eden before any fall or nation (Gen. 2:1-3). God has already named that memorial His SIGN — the sign that He is the LORD who made all and who sanctifies His people (Exo. 31:13-17; Eze. 20:12, 20) — and a sign set in the forehead is a seal: the seal of the living God fixed on His servants before the winds are loosed (Rev. 7:2-3), the Father's name written within (Rev. 14:1), typed by the mark set on the men that sigh and cry over abomination before the slaying begins at the sanctuary (Eze. 9:4-6). The third angel names the two companies plainly: mark-bearers who worship the beast, and saints who "keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus" (Rev. 14:9-12; TMR 112.1) — and the testimony confirms what the verses built: "The Sabbath will be the great test of loyalty," one class receiving the mark of the beast, the other the seal of God (GC 605.2; 8T 117.4; Ev 235.2), a knowledge of God no civil law can enforce (SSP 132.2). Then the door shuts: "he that is holy, let him be holy still" (Rev. 22:11) — the distinction, made visible at last, is made permanent by judgment. Two altars, two names in the forehead, two classes — and after the sealing, no third.

Symbols defined here:

  • the seal of God = the Creator's sign of ownership and sanctification set in the forehead — the seventh-day Sabbath kept by faith; God's own "sign" that He is the LORD who made heaven and earth and who sanctifies His people, marking the separate class before the judgment falls (Rev. 7:2-3; Rev. 14:1; Exo. 31:13-17; Exo. 20:8-11; Gen. 2:1-3; Eze. 20:12, 20; Eze. 9:4).
  • the mark of the beast = allegiance to the self-appointed worship-system enforced in place of the Creator's appointed worship — the way of Cain grown to world scale; received in forehead or hand, set opposite "the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus," and enforced by the decree that "no man might buy or sell" (Rev. 13:16-17; Rev. 14:9-11; Rev. 14:12; Rev. 13:3-4; Rev. 14:7).

Symbols carried: the way of Cain and the two offerings — the self-chosen worship against the appointed lamb, here full grown into the mark (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"); the enmity and the two seeds, now in their last, visible array (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall"); the institutions of Eden — the Sabbath of Gen. 2:1-3, the last of the three under attack (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); the city-system whose confederated commerce becomes the buy-or-sell siege (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"; see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); pilgrims and strangers, the class the siege is aimed at (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"); the days of the Son of man, the heedless age in which the sealing quietly closes and whose mingling judgment ends (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling"); the church-world union that supplanted the appointed day (see "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith"). The summons that gathers the sealed out of Babylon before the plagues is the study's close (see "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call").

For discussion:

  1. The seal and the mark are both set in the FOREHEAD (Rev. 7:3; Rev. 13:16) — but only the mark may also go in the HAND (Rev. 13:16). What does that difference teach about the two allegiances — and why can "no civil law can enforce Sabbath keeping" (SSP 132.2) while a decree CAN produce compliance of the hand, knowingly given (Ev 235.2)?
  2. Ezekiel's type puts its mark — the seal-type — on "the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations" (Eze. 9:4), and the slaying "begin[s] at my sanctuary" (Eze. 9:6). If the sealing distinguishes mourners from the comfortable INSIDE the professed people of God, what am I sighing and crying over now — and what am I comfortable with?
  3. The mark is received by those who obey the decree "while you know that there is not a word in the Bible" behind it (Ev 235.2), and the siege says "no man might buy or sell" without it (Rev. 13:17). What would it cost you, concretely — income, standing, security — to stand with them "that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus" (Rev. 14:12), and what are you doing now so that the cost is already counted before Rev. 22:11 fixes the classes forever?

Part V — Come Out

¶12. Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call

Every separation in this study — the ark door, the angels' hands on Lot, Abraham's "get thee out," the woman's flight to the wilderness — gathers at last into one voice from heaven, "Come out of her, my people"; those who obey take up the pilgrim confession of the whole cloud of witnesses, and the two classes end at two cities: Babylon thrown down, and the New Jerusalem coming down.

The last separation-call — a voice from heaven to MY PEOPLE — Rev. 18:1-4:

  • Rev. 18:1. "And after these things I saw another angel come down from heaven, having great power; and the earth was lightened with his glory" — the closing scene opens with light, not doom: before Babylon falls, the whole earth is lightened, that the call which follows may be heard by every soul still inside.
  • Rev. 18:2. "And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird" — the city of Cain in its end-form: Babylon, the serpent-seed's confederated city-system (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"), become at last what it tended toward from Cain's first wall — the habitation of devils. The city that began with a fugitive from God's presence ends as the cage of every unclean bird.
  • Rev. 18:3. "For all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth are waxed rich through the abundance of her delicacies" — the mingling gone universal: all nations drunk, kings in alliance, merchants enriched (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"). No one is outside her by geography; the only way out of Babylon is the way of the call.
  • Rev. 18:4. "And I heard another voice from heaven, saying, Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues" — the last separation-call of the whole study, addressed to MY PEOPLE — God still has a people INSIDE Babylon. Two mercies attach to the coming out: that they partake not of her sins, and that they receive not of her plagues — and the call sounds before the plagues fall on the marked class (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible").
  • GC 604.1. White: "But God still has a people in Babylon; and before the visitation of His judgments these faithful ones must be called out... the call is heard: 'Come out of her, My people'" — the call is present truth, uniting with the third angel's message as "the final warning to be given to the inhabitants of the earth"; it is spoken to faithful souls yet inside.
  • BP2 69.3. Bates: "the cry is made in the Protestant churches, 'Come out of her, my people.' What is now the response? Thousands on thousands dissolve their connection" — the historical fact: the come-out cry sounded audibly in the 1844 Advent movement and was answered; "the last, and crowning test which God ever gave his people to come away and separate themselves."

Every earlier call was this call — the ark door, the mountain, the tent, the wilderness — Gen. 7:1; 19:17; 12:1; Rev. 12:6:

  • Gen. 7:1. "Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation" — the first "come": the righteous called IN while the world is left out. The ark door is "Come out of her, my people" in its first, physical form — one door dividing two classes (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack").
  • Gen. 19:17. "Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed" — the angels' hands on Lot: flee the doomed city, no lingering, no backward look. The mountain answers the plain — the geography of the two classes from the beginning (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"; "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain").
  • Gen. 12:1. "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee" — Abraham's "get thee out," the call that made him father of the faithful; the covenant people begin with a come-out, separation from country and kindred toward a land not yet seen.
  • Rev. 12:6. "And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days" — the true church kept by flight through the mingled centuries: the woman flees the city-power exactly as Lot fled to the mountain, and God prepares her place (see "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith"). The come-out class has never been without a prepared refuge.
  • MWV2 266.5. Miller: "God has called his people into the wilderness state, time and again. 1st. Abraham was called to go out from the land of his fathers 'into a strange land'... for he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose Builder and Maker is God" — the pioneer reading: the come-out-into-the-wilderness pattern runs from Abraham forward, and the pilgrim's eye is on the city God builds.
  • GC 65.3. White: "Behind the lofty bulwarks of the mountains—in all ages the refuge of the persecuted and oppressed—the Waldenses found a hiding place... Here, for a thousand years, witnesses for the truth maintained the ancient faith" — the historical anchor: the mountain class of Gen. 19:17 and Rev. 12:6 walked through history, and the truth was kept a thousand years by the separated — "witnesses for the truth" in the very cloud of Heb. 12:1.

Separation is a settled law — and its reward is adoption — Isa. 52:11; 2 Cor. 6:14-18:

  • Isa. 52:11. "Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD" — the Old Testament root of both texts that follow: going out of her midst and touching no unclean thing is a settled law of God's people, not a novelty of the last message. Note the reason attached — "that bear the vessels of the LORD": the separated are separated FOR service.
  • 2 Cor. 6:14. "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?" — the unequal yoke is the very mingling by which the peculiar people lost their peculiarity (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); the questions admit no third answer.
  • 2 Cor. 6:15-16. "And what concord hath Christ with Belial?... ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" — the ground of the separation: the believer is God's dwelling; the temple cannot be yoked to idols. "They shall be my people" — the same "my people" the voice from heaven addresses in Babylon.
  • 2 Cor. 6:17. "Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you" — Isa. 52:11 quoted into the church: God's reception is conditioned on the coming out. He does not receive a people still yoked to Babylon.
  • 2 Cor. 6:18. "And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty" — separation is not loss but ADOPTION. What Babylon calls exile, heaven calls a family; the unequal yoke forfeits the sonship, the come-out receives it.

The pilgrim confession — the cloud of witnesses and the better country — Heb. 11:13-16; 12:1; 13:14:

  • Heb. 11:13. "These all died in faith, not having received the promises... and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth" — one confession on every tongue in this study: Abel at his altar, Enoch walking with God, Noah in the ark, Abraham in his tent, the church in the wilderness — the pilgrims-and-strangers identity (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain").
  • Heb. 11:14. "For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country" — the confession is a declaration: to confess "stranger here" is to declare "citizen there."
    • the better country = the heavenly inheritance every pilgrim witness confessed and sought — God's answer to the man-built city of Cain; not any place on this earth, for "here have we no continuing city," but the prepared city to come (Heb. 11:14; Heb. 11:16; Heb. 13:14). Defined in full at the close.
  • Heb. 11:15. "And truly, if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned" — the come-out is kept in the MIND: the road back stood open all their lives, and the pilgrims refused it. Lot's wife took it — the backward look that unmade an escape (Gen. 19:17, 26; see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling").
  • Heb. 11:16. "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city" — the desire names the class, and God answers the desire with a CITY. Man built the first city in rebellion; God builds the last one for the pilgrims — and He is "not ashamed" to be the God of pilgrims; He owns no other class.
  • Heb. 12:1. "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us" — the seal on the whole arc: the reader now stands compassed about by every come-out witness of the study and is summoned to run the same separated, pilgrim race.
  • Heb. 13:14. "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come" — the pilgrim confession stated as doctrine: no continuing city HERE — not Cain's city of Enoch (Gen. 4:17), not Babel, not Sodom, not Babylon. The seed of the woman seeks the one to come.
  • PP 81.1. White: Cain stands "at the head of that great class of men who worship the god of this world," while Abel led a pastoral life, and the descendants of Seth followed the same course, "counting themselves 'strangers and pilgrims on the earth,' seeking 'a better country, that is, an heavenly.' Hebrews 11:13, 16" — the two classes at the fountainhead named in EGW's own words, from this very spine text: the pilgrim confession is as old as the second generation from Eden.
  • PP 170.2. White: "We must dwell as pilgrims and strangers here if we would gain 'a better country, that is, an heavenly'... Those who are children of Abraham will be seeking the city which he looked for, 'whose builder and maker is God'" — the confession made present-tense: to gain the country, dwell as pilgrims now.

The come-out class named — peculiar, priestly, at war with the flesh — Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:9-11:

  • Titus 2:14. "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works" — the purpose of the cross is a purified, PECULIAR people (the covenant identity itself, see "Israel Mingles — 'Like All the Nations'"); the separation is not idleness in the mountain but zeal in good works — separated FOR service, as Isa. 52:11's vessel-bearers.
  • 1 Pet. 2:9. "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light" — the identity in full, and its verb: a people CALLED OUT — of darkness into light — for the purpose of witness. The come-out class exists to shew forth His praises, not to hide.
  • 1 Pet. 2:10. "Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy" — the "my people" of Rev. 18:4 defined: made a people by mercy, not by blood or city; no one is born inside it, and no one still yoked to Babylon is outside its reach.
  • 1 Pet. 2:11. "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul" — the pilgrim confession bound to appetite: the very "eating and drinking" indulgence that marked the heedless antediluvian class wars against the pilgrim soul (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack").
  • CD 379.2. White: "Our habits of eating and drinking show whether we are of the world or among the number whom the Lord by His mighty cleaver of truth has separated from the world. These are His peculiar people, zealous of good works" — the separation made visible at the table; Titus 2:14 and 1 Pet. 2:9 joined to a real, present distinction, and the "cleaver of truth" is the Lord's own.
  • AA 109.4. White: the members of God's church are "to be zealous of good works, separating from worldly ambition and walking in the footsteps of Him who went about doing good" — set apart FOR good works, not merely apart.
  • CG 449.3. White: "Our only safety is to stand as God's peculiar people... making no compromise with its corrupt and idolatrous practices" — the peculiar identity as the ONLY safety: no inch yielded — the come-out call lived out daily.

Two cities end the study — one thrown down, one coming down — Rev. 18:20-21; 21:2:

  • Rev. 18:20. "Rejoice over her, thou heaven, and ye holy apostles and prophets; for God hath avenged you on her" — heaven's verdict on the city that persecuted the pilgrim class from righteous Abel forward (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"): avenged.
  • Rev. 18:21. "And a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying, Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all" — the end of the first city: the city-system Cain began and Nimrod raised again at Babel is "found no more at all." This is the urgency of the call — the city cannot be reformed, only left.
    • the two cities = the two destinations of the two classes: Babylon, the end-form of the city of Cain, "become the habitation of devils" and thrown down to be found no more; and the New Jerusalem, the city God "hath prepared" for the pilgrims, coming down from God out of heaven (Rev. 18:2; Rev. 18:21; Rev. 21:2; Heb. 11:16). Defined in full at the close.
  • Rev. 21:2. "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband" — the end of the second city: the pilgrims who sought a country receive a city; "he hath prepared for them a city" (Heb. 11:16) kept to the letter. Note the directions: Babylon is thrown DOWN; the New Jerusalem comes DOWN — one city falls by judgment, the other descends as a gift.
  • COL 152.1. White: "The Pharisee and the publican represent two great classes... Their first two representatives are found in the first two children that were born into the world" — the thesis of the whole study confirmed at its close: from the first two children born to the last two cities standing, there are two classes, and only two; the come-out call is where the reader chooses between them.

DEFINITION — COME OUT, MY PEOPLE — THE PILGRIM CALL = the last form of every separation this study has traced. The voice from heaven — "Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues" (Rev. 18:4) — is the ark door of Noah ("Come thou... into the ark," Gen. 7:1), the angels' hands on Lot ("escape to the mountain," Gen. 19:17), Abraham's "Get thee out" (Gen. 12:1), and the woman's flight to the wilderness (Rev. 12:6) spoken once more, worldwide, to God's OWN people still inside Babylon — the city of Cain "become the habitation of devils" (Rev. 18:2; GC 604.1). It is no novelty but a settled law: "go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean" (Isa. 52:11), "come out from among them, and be ye separate" (2 Cor. 6:17) — and its reward is not exile but ADOPTION: "And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters" (2 Cor. 6:18) — the unequal yoke forfeits the sonship, the separation receives it. The whole cloud of witnesses seals the call: every witness of the study "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb. 11:13; PP 81.1), refused the open road back (Heb. 11:15), and desired "a better country, that is, an heavenly" — wherefore God, "not ashamed to be called their God... hath prepared for them a city" (Heb. 11:16; Heb. 13:14; PP 170.2) — and the reader, "compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses" (Heb. 12:1) — Abel at his altar, Enoch walking with God, Noah at the ark door, Abraham in his tent, the woman in the wilderness, the Waldenses behind the mountains (GC 65.3; MWV2 266.5) — is summoned to run the same race. The come-out class is Christ's own purchase, "a peculiar people, zealous of good works" (Titus 2:14), "called... out of darkness into his marvellous light," beseeched "as strangers and pilgrims" to abstain from the fleshly lusts of the heedless line (1 Pet. 2:9-11; CD 379.2; CG 449.3) — separated from the world's ambition and appetite, and separated FOR service. The testimony fixes it as present truth — "God still has a people in Babylon... these faithful ones must be called out" (GC 604.1) — and history proves it a cry that has already sounded once and was answered by thousands, when in 1844 "thousands on thousands" dissolved their connection at the call (BP2 69.3). And the study ends where the two classes end — at two cities: Babylon "thrown down... found no more at all" (Rev. 18:21), the holy city "coming down from God out of heaven" (Rev. 21:2). One city falls; one descends. From the first two children born into the world (COL 152.1; PP 81.1) the classes have been two and only two; the pilgrim call sets the choice before every soul — which seed, which city, which class.

Symbols defined here:

  • the better country = the heavenly inheritance every pilgrim witness of the study confessed and sought — God's answer to the man-built city of Cain; those who came out refused to return, "desire a better country, that is, an heavenly," and receive the city God prepared, for "here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come" (Heb. 11:13-16; Heb. 13:14; PP 170.2).
  • the two cities = the two destinations of the two classes: Babylon, the end-form of the city of Cain — "the habitation of devils," thrown down and "found no more at all" — and the New Jerusalem, the prepared city, "coming down from God out of heaven"; the come-out call sets every reader between them (Rev. 18:2; Rev. 18:21; Rev. 21:2; Heb. 11:16).

Symbols carried: Babel / Babylon, the confederated city-system here reaching its fall (see "Babel — Congregating for Convenience"); the city of Cain and the mountains-and-plains geography that Gen. 19:17 replays (see "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name"); the two worships from the first two altars, avenged at last in Rev. 18:20 (see "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships"); the mingling / the unequal yoke that Rev. 18:3 shows gone universal (see "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity"); pilgrims and strangers, the confessed identity of Heb. 11:13, with the tent and the altar against the plain (see "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain"); the peculiar people, the covenant identity restored in Titus 2:14 and 1 Pet. 2:9 (see "Israel Mingles — 'Like All the Nations'"); the woman and the wilderness of Rev. 12:6 (see "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith"); eating and drinking / the fleshly lusts of 1 Pet. 2:11 (see "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack"); the backward look of Lot's wife, the escape unmade (see "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling"); the plagues from which the come-out delivers, falling on the marked class (see "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible"); and the two seeds themselves, whose God-put enmity this call consummates (see "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall").

For discussion:

  1. The voice of Rev. 18:4 is addressed to "MY PEOPLE" — God owns them as His even while they stand in the wrong city — and 2 Cor. 6:17-18 promises that the one who comes out is received as a son or daughter. What does that say about how we regard souls still in Babylon — and if separation is adoption and not loss, what makes remaining feel safer than coming out?
  2. The pilgrims "might have had opportunity to have returned" (Heb. 11:15) yet refused to be "mindful of that country," while Lot's wife left the city with her body and kept it in her heart (Gen. 19:17, 26). Since the come-out is kept in the mind and the desire (Heb. 11:16), where does your own "opportunity to return" still stand open — and what would it mean this week to stop being "mindful of that country" you came out of?
  3. The come-out class is "a peculiar people, zealous of good works" (Titus 2:14), called out of darkness "that ye should shew forth the praises of him" (1 Pet. 2:9) — separated FOR witness, not merely FROM the city. How do you tell the difference, in practice, between a separation that shews forth His praises and a withdrawal that merely hides — and which city does each one serve?

¶Appendix — Symbol Dictionary

Every symbol defined in this handbook, alphabetically (leading articles ignored), with its receipts and owning section.

  • Abel's offering (the firstlings of his flock) = the appointed lamb brought by faith — righteousness by faith enacted at the world's first altar, the firstling's blood confessing the coming Lamb of God who takes away sin; accepted because it comes God's appointed way, trusting wholly in the promised atonement (Gen. 4:4; Heb. 11:4; John 1:29; Gen. 3:15). — defined in "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships".
  • Babel / Babylon = the serpent-seed's confederated city-system: congregation for convenience and self-security in defiance of God's command to fill the earth, and self-naming in defiance of calling on the Name of the LORD; founded by Nimrod on the plain of Shinar, named CONFUSION by God's judgment, and carried forward by the Spirit to "Babylon the great" (Gen. 11:4; Gen. 11:8-9; Gen. 10:8-10; Gen. 9:1; Gen. 4:26; Rev. 17:5). — defined in "Babel — Congregating for Convenience".
  • the better country = the heavenly inheritance every pilgrim witness of the study confessed and sought — God's answer to the man-built city of Cain; those who came out refused to return, "desire a better country, that is, an heavenly," and receive the city God prepared, for "here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come" (Heb. 11:13-16; Heb. 13:14; PP 170.2). — defined in "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call".
  • Cain's offering (the fruit of the ground) = will-worship: the self-chosen, bloodless way substituted for God's appointed way — the first false worship; partial obedience (an altar, a gift) that omits the essential thing, faith in the promised Redeemer's blood, and comes in the worshiper's own merits, and to which God has not respect (Gen. 4:3; Gen. 4:5; Gen. 4:7; Col. 2:23). — defined in "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships".
  • calling on the name of the LORD = the dividing act of the faithful seed — open, avowed worship, a public profession of loyalty that marks off the Sethite line from the city; crowned in Enoch, who walked with God in the corrupt age and preached judgment to the city of Cain (Gen. 4:26; Gen. 5:24; Jude 1:14-15; PP 80.2). — defined in "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name".
  • the city of Cain = the serpent-seed's congregation — fortified convenience built by the fugitive from God's presence; man staying put in the cursed earth, distinguished in arts, industry, and violence-as-culture while God is forgotten; the civilization whose spirit prevails in the eating-drinking-marrying world Christ names as the type of the last age (Gen. 4:16-17; Gen. 4:21-23; Matt. 24:38; PP 81.1). — defined in "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name".
  • the daughters of men = the Cainite line, the world — the daughters of the multiplying "men" of Gen. 6:1, the class of the man who went out from the presence of the LORD, already practicing polygamy (Gen. 6:1-2; Gen. 4:16; Gen. 4:19). — defined in "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity".
  • the days of the Son of man = the last age, defined by Christ through the matched Noah/Lot pattern — heedless absorption in lawful things (eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building), mingled worship as the covenant line blends with the world, and sudden separation by judgment on "the same day" the righteous go out; the mark of the age is "knew not" (Luke 17:26-30; Matt. 24:37-39; Gen. 6:2, 5; Gen. 13:12-13). — defined in "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling".
  • the doctrine of Balaam = corrupting by mingling what cannot be cursed — the serpent's standing strategy against the peculiar people; barred from cursing from without, Balaam counsels the daughters, the feasts, and the worship of Moab, so the people curse themselves by their own transgression; Christ names it a permanent doctrine and finds it held in a New Testament church (Num. 31:16; Num. 25:1-3; Num. 23:9; Rev. 2:14). — defined in "Israel Mingles — "Like All the Nations"".
  • dwelling alone = the appointed posture of the woman's seed among the nations — separation as safety, not isolation as loss; Balaam's own mouth confesses the people "shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations," Moses seals it as "dwell in safety alone," and the demand for a king "like all the nations" is the deliberate reversal of the posture (Num. 23:9; Deut. 33:28; 1 Sam. 8:5, 20). — defined in "Israel Mingles — "Like All the Nations"".
  • eating and drinking = Christ's mark of the heedless class before the flood: lawful appetite — eating, drinking, marrying — made the whole of life, so that the ordinary swallowed the eternal and men "knew not" until judgment fell; not gross crime but total absorption in the permitted, the sign of a world that has erased the distinction between the holy and the common (Matt. 24:38-39; Luke 17:27). — defined in "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack".
  • the enmity = the God-put antagonism between the two seeds — grace, not curse: fallen man is naturally at peace with the serpent, so "I will put enmity" is a supernatural interposition of implanted grace, creating "conflict where hitherto had been peace"; to lose it by befriending the world is to become "the enemy of God," and the world's hatred of the saints is the same enmity running outward (Gen. 3:15; Jas. 4:4; John 15:19; GC 505.2; GC 506.2). — defined in "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall".
  • having a form of godliness = the last-days condition inside the church: an outward shape of religion emptied of its power, the professed mingled with the world in appetite and pleasure while keeping the exterior of piety — the Noah/Lot mingling relocated from the world into the sanctuary, Laodicea "rich, and increased with goods" yet "knowest not" (2 Tim. 3:1-5; Rev. 3:17; Matt. 24:39). — defined in "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling".
  • the institutions of Eden = the three gifts God established before sin: MARRIAGE (one man and one woman made one flesh), the APPOINTED DIET (the seed-bearing bounty given for meat), and the SABBATH (the seventh day blessed and sanctified) — all three predating the fall, all three assaulted by the serpent's seed: polygamy against marriage, indulgence against the diet, self-appointed worship against the appointed, the last war ending at the Sabbath (Gen. 2:24; Gen. 1:29; Gen. 2:1-3; Gen. 4:19; Gen. 6:2). — defined in "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack".
  • the mark of the beast = allegiance to the self-appointed worship-system enforced in place of the Creator's appointed worship — the way of Cain grown to world scale; received in forehead or hand, set opposite "the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus," and enforced by the decree that "no man might buy or sell" (Rev. 13:16-17; Rev. 14:9-11; Rev. 14:12; Rev. 13:3-4; Rev. 14:7). — defined in "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible".
  • the mingling = the alliance of the two classes by which the peculiar people lose their peculiarity — the standing mechanism of apostasy: choice by sight, union with the world, one-directional descent, ending in "all flesh had corrupted his way"; forbidden as the unequal yoke, named as the friendship of the world (Gen. 6:1-5; Gen. 6:12; 2 Cor. 6:14; 1 Cor. 15:33; Jas. 4:4). — defined in "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity".
  • mountains and plains = the geography of the two classes — the serpent's seed congregating over the plains and valleys for convenience, the faithful withdrawing to the mountains to keep their peculiar character and their worship pure; the geography of separation, not of appointed worship, given its biblical voice in "Escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed" (Gen. 4:16; Gen. 6:1-2; Gen. 19:17; PP 81.2; GC 65.3). — defined in "The Two Lineages — the City and the Name".
  • the original diet = the Gen. 1:29 grant — fruits, grains, herbs, and after the fall the herb of the field — with flesh not granted until after the flood, so that the vegetable grant stood through the whole antediluvian age and the days-of-Noah appetite ran against, not within, God's appointment (Gen. 1:29; Gen. 3:18; Gen. 9:3). — defined in "The Days of Noah — the Institutions of Eden Under Attack".
  • peculiar people = God's purchased, set-apart treasure — distinctness is not an accessory to the covenant identity, it IS the covenant identity; Israel is a "peculiar treasure above all people" and "a kingdom of priests" precisely by keeping the covenant that unlikes them from the nations, and the same charter passes unchanged to the church redeemed by Christ's blood; to be conformed is to forfeit the identity (Exo. 19:5-6; Deut. 14:2; Deut. 7:6; Titus 2:14; 1 Pet. 2:9). — defined in "Israel Mingles — "Like All the Nations"".
  • the plain of Sodom = choice by sight — the well-watered convenience, "as the garden of the LORD," chosen with the eyes and no altar named, ending inside the doomed city by one unbroken drift: toward, in, gate (Gen. 13:10-13; Gen. 14:12; Gen. 19:1). — defined in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain".
  • Remember Lot's wife = the last-generation warning against a divided separation — out of the city with the body, in it with the heart; she obeyed the call to come out, and one backward look fixed her forever as the standing type of the professor whose separation never reached the affections (Luke 17:32; Gen. 19:26; Gen. 13:12-13). — defined in "As in the Days of Noah — the Last Mingling".
  • the seal of God = the Creator's sign of ownership and sanctification set in the forehead — the seventh-day Sabbath kept by faith; God's own "sign" that He is the LORD who made heaven and earth and who sanctifies His people, marking the separate class before the judgment falls (Rev. 7:2-3; Rev. 14:1; Exo. 31:13-17; Exo. 20:8-11; Gen. 2:1-3; Eze. 20:12, 20; Eze. 9:4). — defined in "The Seal or the Mark — the Distinction Made Visible".
  • the seed of the serpent = a spiritual paternity, not a bloodline — those who belong to the devil by doing his works: "of your father the devil" by doing his lusts, "the children of the wicked one" sown as tares, Cain "of that wicked one" though Eve's own son; the test is practice — "he that committeth sin is of the devil," "whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God" (John 8:44; Matt. 13:38-39; 1 John 3:12; 1 John 3:8; 1 John 3:10). — defined in "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall".
  • the seed of the woman = Christ first, and in Him His people — the singular seed "which is Christ," reckoned to all who are Christ's, sown by the Son of man as the children of the kingdom, sharing the head-bruising victory, and terminating in "the remnant of her seed" who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus (Gen. 3:15; Gal. 3:16; Gal. 3:29; Matt. 13:37-38; Rom. 16:20; Rev. 12:17). — defined in "The Enmity — Two Seeds from One Fall".
  • the sons of God = the covenant line of Seth, the professed people of God — Scripture's own idiom for Adam's faithful line ("the son of God," Luke 3:38) and the covenant people ("the children of the LORD your God," Deut. 14:1); read literally, not angels, for angels marry not (Gen. 6:2; Luke 3:38; Deut. 14:1-2; Matt. 22:30). — defined in "The Mingling — How the Peculiar People Lost Their Peculiarity".
  • strangers and pilgrims = the confessed identity of the woman's seed in every age — those who own that earth is not home and declare plainly that they seek a better, heavenly country; Abraham the pattern, the church the heir of the title (Heb. 11:13-16; 1 Pet. 2:11; Gen. 12:1). — defined in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain".
  • the tent and the altar = the pilgrim life — dwelling loose from the world with worship at the center, portable, needing no city or temple; an altar at every pitch, because worship is bound to spirit and truth, not to a place, and the tent confesses that home is the city God builds (Gen. 12:7-8; Gen. 13:4, 18; Heb. 11:9-10; John 4:23-24). — defined in "Abraham and Lot — the Tent and the Plain".
  • the tower = man-made security against God's judgment and against His command to scatter and fill the earth — brick-and-slime presumption trusted for the safety and the name that belong to the LORD alone, exposed by the LORD's "coming down" and answered by the confusion of tongues and the very scattering it was built to prevent (Gen. 11:3-5; Gen. 11:8). — defined in "Babel — Congregating for Convenience".
  • the two cities = the two destinations of the two classes: Babylon, the end-form of the city of Cain — "the habitation of devils," thrown down and "found no more at all" — and the New Jerusalem, the prepared city, "coming down from God out of heaven"; the come-out call sets every reader between them (Rev. 18:2; Rev. 18:21; Rev. 21:2; Heb. 11:16). — defined in "Come Out, My People — the Pilgrim Call".
  • the way of Cain = self-appointed worship that hardens into a lineage and ends in persecuting the true — the false worshiper hating and slaying the true because his own works are evil and his brother's righteous; the pattern that opens the martyr stream from righteous Abel onward (Jude 1:11; 1 John 3:12; Gen. 4:8; Matt. 23:35). — defined in "Cain and Abel — the Two Worships".
  • the wilderness = the place of preservation-by-separation for the true church during the mingled centuries — a condition, not a geography: God's provided refuge, entered by flight and not conquest, where the woman is fed away from the serpent through the 1260 days/years; needing no cathedral because worship is "in spirit and in truth," and located by Scripture itself "in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth" (Rev. 12:6, 14; Heb. 11:38; John 4:23-24; 2 Cor. 6:17). — defined in "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith".
  • the woman = the true church, the seed of the woman corporate — the pure bride of Christ, kept distinct by loyalty rather than numbers; God likens the daughter of Zion to a woman, Christ loves the church as a husband his wife "not having spot," and her remnant seed keep the commandments of God and the testimony of Jesus, over against the harlot Babylon who married the world (Jer. 6:2; Rev. 12:1-2, 17; Eph. 5:25, 27; Rev. 17:5). — defined in "The Church in the Wilderness — the Mountains Keep the Faith".
The Sure Word — Bible handbook studies. Every line: reference → text → gloss. "We have also a more sure word of prophecy" — 2 Peter 1:19
